Furthermore, the grain-boundary-associated geometrically necessary dislocations (GND) provide a local, upper-bound strengthening increment of ∼173 MPa. This study demonstrates that interface-controlled twin–slip interactions and GND accumulations play an essential role in achieving concurrent high strength, ductility, and strain compatibility in lamellar near-α Zr alloys.

title: Correlation between enhanced oxygen evolution and β→γ phase transition in Mn-doped NiOOH
abstract: NiOOH is a promising electrocatalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Here we systematically investigate the effect of Mn doping on the structure, oxidation state, bond length, phase transition, and OER activity of NiOOH using dispersion-corrected hybrid density functional theory (HSE06+D3) combined with experimental material characterization and electrochemical measurements for samples that were prepared through a synthesis route mimicking Ni recovery from wastewater with circular-material benefits. Our results reveal that Mn doping promotes not only the formation of surface oxygen vacancies but also the phase transition from β- to γ-NiOOH, a critical step overlooked by previous studies. This Mn-doping is found to largely reduce the calculated overpotential, especially with respect to undoped β system, in very good agreement with experimental observations.

title: Solid/liquid interface energy and its anisotropy of pure metals
abstract: Solid/liquid (S/L) interface energy ( γ sl ) and its anisotropy ( φ ) play a critical role in the understanding of nearly every single phenomenon that occurs during solidification of metals, such as nucleation, morphological instability and dendrite growth. However, due to difficulties associated with both experimental measurement and computer simulations, our current understanding of this topic is rather limited. In this work, a simple analytical model is developed to predict γ sl and φ for pure metals. This model suggests that S/L interface energy originates from atomic ordering in the S/L interface templated by the solid. γ sl can be expressed as the sum of contributions from both atomic layering ( γ z ) and the in-plane atomic ordering ( γ xy ). Further analysis shows that γ sl for pure metals is determined by both heat of fusion per atom ( Δ H f a ) and their crystal structures, while anisotropy depends only on crystal structure. The analytical model reveals that the physical origin of γ sl is atomic ordering in the S/L interface templated by the solid, while the physical origin of anisotropy is the difference in structural templating power between different crystal planes. It is demonstrated that the current analytical model is capable of predicting solid/liquid interface energy ( γ sl ) and its anisotropy ( φ ) for any metallic element using parameters readily available in the literature.

title: Valence-electron-associated dislocation dissociation and glide mechanisms in transition-metal carbide and nitride alloys
abstract: Conventional and high-entropy alloying are widely employed to mitigate the intrinsic brittleness of transition-metal carbides (TMCs) and nitrides (TMNs), yet the underlying dislocation-controlled mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this work, we developed a new approach to determine the Peierls stress within the Peierls-Nabarro framework, and investigated the stacking fault energies and associated dislocation properties of pure TMCs, TMNs, and their alloys. For compounds with valence electron concentration (VEC) exceeding 8 electrons per formula unit (e - /f.u.), full a / 2 〈 110 〉 { 111 } dislocations dissociate into Shockley partials, enabling stepwise glide, substantially reducing the Peierls stress, and thereby facilitating activation of the 〈110〉{111} slip system, consistent with experimental observations. For compounds with VEC ≤8 e - /f.u., the absence of an intrinsic stacking fault suppresses dislocation dissociation, resulting in large Peierls stresses. Extending these insights to both conventional and high-entropy alloys, higher-VEC solutes promote dissociation and reduce the Peierls stress, whereas lower-VEC solutes exert the opposite effect, and same-group element doping has only a minor influence. These findings lay the groundwork for elucidating the dislocation-relevant mechanism underlying alloying-induced tailoring of mechanical performance in TMC and TMN alloys.

title: Anisotropic deformation and material removal mechanisms of p-type 4H-SiC
Domain boundary induced crack deflection enhancing the toughness of lamellar TiAl alloys
Engineering diffusion pathways for simultaneous solid-solution formation and grain refinement in Mo-Nb alloys
Explaining hydrogen-accelerated high temperature creep using the defactant theory
abstract: We propose a quantitative description of creep acceleration in gaseous hydrogen environment. The central hypothesis is that hydrogen enhances high temperature creep by reducing the vacancy formation energy, thereby facilitating faster dislocation climb. By employing the defactant theory, we derive the ratio of steady-state creep strain rate in gaseous hydrogen ε ˙ H to creep rate in the absence of hydrogen ε ˙ as ε ˙ H / ε ˙ = ( 1 − Γ / Γ max ) − Γ max , where Γ is the number of hydrogen atoms trapped at a vacancy and Γ max is the maximum number of hydrogen atoms that can be trapped by a vacancy. We demonstrate the predictive capability of the proposed model by comparing with experimental measurements of creep strain rates across a range of hydrogen pressures and temperatures. Notably, this defactant-theory based formulation of creep law introduces no additional fitting parameters and is defined entirely by physically well-established quantities.

title: A phase field model of the effects of dislocation microstructure on grain boundary motion during recrystallization
abstract: The internal energy associated with the defect microstructure of strongly deformed crystals provides an important driving force for grain boundary motion during recrystallization. Typical dislocation microstructures are strongly heterogeneous and this heterogeneity affects the motion of recrystallization boundaries. In this study, a phase field model for microstructure evolution encompassing the evolution of both dislocation densities and grain order parameters is formulated. The model is employed to generate typical dislocation microstructures exhibiting multiscale features such as incidental and geometrically necessary dislocation walls. It is then used to study the motion of recrystallization boundaries in the associated complex defect energy ‘landscape’. Results are compared to experimental observations.

title: Terahertz oscillation of 180° domain walls in ferroelectric membranes
Amorphization-induced metallic-bonded heterointerface for ampere-level alkaline hydrogen evolution
Competing adsorption of H and CO on Pd-alloy surfaces:Mechanistic insight into the mitigating effect of Cu on CO poisoning
abstract: Multi-component alloys offer broad tunability for materials science applications, but are highly sensitive to operating conditions through adsorption and segregation phenomena. Here, we study Pd–Au–Cu alloy surfaces in H 2 and CO environments motivated by their use in H technologies, where alloying can mitigate limitations intrinsic to Pd such as CO poisoning. To this end, we establish a framework combining machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on density-functional theory data with cluster expansions, with effectively no limitations on training set size. By constructing continuous surface phase diagrams for H–CO coadsorption, we find that adsorption under operating conditions is governed by the H coverage during the preceding annealing. Au-rich surfaces, formed under H-poor conditions, suppress both CO and H adsorption, while H-rich conditions yield Pd-rich surfaces that promote CO and H adsorption. Furthermore, Pd-rich alloy surfaces maintain higher H coverages compared to pure Pd at relevant CO partial pressures, indicating improved CO poisoning resistance. The coadsorption behavior of PdAuCu alloys is indistinguishable from that of PdAu alloys, despite experimental observations of Cu, specifically, mitigating CO poisoning. However, kinetic barriers of H sorption in dilute alloys indicate that H pathways near Au are highly unfavorable, while Cu leaves the energetics unchanged compared to pure Pd. Based on these findings and the experimental evidence, we hypothesize that alloying promotes H adsorption while Cu, specifically, preserves viable H absorption pathways in the presence of CO.

title: Cr-mediated modulation of κ-phase shearability and stacking fault energy enabling hetero-deformation strengthening in CoNiV-based multi-principal element alloys
Evolution of radiation-induced grain boundary segregation in an ion irradiated Fe-Ni-Cr alloy undergoing spinodal decomposition
abstract: Radiation-induced segregation (RIS) is a non-equilibrium phenomenon that is observed in irradiated alloys and results from the interactions of solute atoms and point defects at defect sinks such as grain boundaries. RIS is often considered to reach a steady state behavior at relatively low doses. However, using two model Fe-Ni-Cr alloys that were ion irradiated at 400 °C, we show that the evolution of RIS at grain boundaries correlates with phase evolution in grain interiors. In the alloy undergoing irradiation-accelerated spinodal decomposition, grain boundary chemistry was dominated by RIS at low doses with the expected Ni enrichment and Fe and Cr depletion. RIS, however, evolved significantly at higher doses as phase separation evolved in the grain interior from mid (15 dpa) to high doses (70 dpa). In the second alloy, the extent of the phase separation did not evolve from low (5 dpa) to high dose (70 dpa), correlating with no notable changes in the RIS response at grain boundaries. The findings highlight the synergy between grain interior and grain boundaries during irradiation.

title: Mesoscopic connectivity of second phases regulates long-term oxidation stability in Mg–RE alloys: A topological isolation strategy
Variable-charge model of GaN within the Streitz–Mintmire formalism
Fatigue crack growth of tungsten in the semi-ductile temperature regime
abstract: Tungsten will play an indispensable role for novel fusion reactors due to its exceptional physical properties, however, its low damage tolerance involves risks. Therefore, fracture toughness has been extensively investigated over decades, but the understanding on the resistance against fatigue crack growth remains scarce. In this study, fatigue crack growth and fracture toughness experiments were performed on pure tungsten (ITER-grade) in the semi-ductile temperature regime at 773 K in high vacuum. To account for microstructural anisotropy, different crack plane orientations were investigated, and the impact of shielding effects was examined by varying the load ratio R between 0.1 and 0.7. A central outcome is the unexpected behavior in the threshold regime compared to common metals. Doubling the stress intensity factor barely affected the propagation rate, while in the Paris regime, the rate increased by two orders of magnitude. This behavior is attributed to the changing slip reversibility of dislocations and the rewelding of the crack wake in vacuum. Further findings are the insensitiveness of the crack growth rate against changes of mean stress up to R = 0.5 and the early onset of delamination in the case of fatigue loading, caused by the reversible loading in the cyclic plastic zone. This study constitutes an important step towards elucidating the intrinsic and extrinsic fatigue crack growth mechanisms in tungsten and represents a key milestone in developing safe, damage-tolerant structural tungsten-based components.

title: Geometric effects of inclusions on hydrogen embrittlement in high-strength steel
Duality of wave modulation and nanotwinning in Ni–Mn–Ga martensite via long-period commensurate states
abstract: Structural modulation is a key ingredient behind the extraordinary (magneto)elastic response of Ni–Mn–Ga martensite, yet its link to fine microstructural features and twin-boundary supermobility remains unresolved. Here we analyse martensitic single crystals of Ni 50.0 Mn 27.7 Ga 22.3 and Ni 50.0 Mn 28.1 Ga 21.9 . Neutron and X-ray diffraction reveal an anharmonic five-layer structural modulation—evidenced by high-order satellite reflections—that evolves from commensurate ( q = 2/5) to incommensurate (2/5 < q < 5/12) upon cooling. Interpreting the refined modulation displacements as a basal-plane stacking sequence links the wave description to the microstructural evolution on cooling. In this view, evolving incommensurability produces periodic nanodomains interpreted as emerging a/b -nanotwins with a characteristic size of ≈20 nm at ≈290 K. With further cooling, the modulation can lock into long-period commensurate (LP-C) states, such as 34O ( q = 7/17), 24O ( q = 5/12), and 14O ( q = 3/7), whose orthorhombic unit cells can be viewed as a/b -nanotwins. Ab initio calculations show that LP-C structures are energetically competitive with the initial commensurate state, supporting a shallow martensitic energy landscape. We propose a physical picture in which the martensitic transformation selects a commensurate state with q = 2/5 in the Mn-rich compositions studied here, while subsequent cooling drives relaxation within the martensitic landscape toward LP-C states, particularly 24O in the present alloys. The resulting structure is neither purely wave-like nor purely nanotwinned; rather, it reflects coupling between a coherent modulation wave and local accommodation via NM-like tetragonal distortions, nanotwinning, and LP-C lock-ins, providing a structural basis for the wave–nanotwin duality in Ni–Mn–Ga martensite.

title: Beyond linear elastic fracture mechanics: Atomistic modeling of fracture toughness in silicate glasses via energy landscape sampling
Effects of short-range order on void growth in single-crystalline CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys
Time-resolved evolution of micro-, crystal structure, and temperature field during resonant laser sintering of SnO2 nanoparticles
abstract: The structural evolution of tin dioxide (SnO₂) nanoparticle films during resonant laser sintering is investigated using simultaneous, time-resolved small-angle (SAXS) and wide-angle (WAXS) X-ray scattering combined with high-speed near-infrared (NIR) thermography. A focused synchrotron X-ray beam enables spatially and temporally resolved probing of structural changes at both the microstructural and crystal structure scale. The evolution of the temperature field is monitored to correlate the structural dynamics with the temperature–time profile and to analyze the grain growth kinetics. The structural changes observed in situ are complemented by ex situ scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the evolved microstructure. In addition, the lattice expansion by laser induced heating is determined, and the corresponding thermal expansion coefficients are derived. These space- and time-resolved measurements provide detailed insights into the mechanisms governing resonant laser sintering of SnO₂ nanoparticles.

title: An experimental-based multiscale method for calculating radiation-enhanced mobility in solids: Application to radiation-induced microstructure in FeCr
abstract: By combining MD simulations with a Phase Field approach, this work enables the modeling of radiationinduced microstructures based on the minimization of a quasi-potential  within the framework of macroscopic fluctuation theory. The methodology we propose is an alternative way to bypass the difficulty of calculating the radiation-enhanced mobilities. The model we propose is validated by a direct comparison between simulated and experimental microstructures extracted from APT measurements performed on an ultra-pure alloy concentrated in Fe 0.81 Cr 0.19 irradiated with 2 MeV Fe ions at different temperatures and fluxes. This work is able to explain flux effects observed in this materials and can be easily extended for modeling microstructures induced by neutron flux paving the way for the simulation of radiation-induced microstructures in nuclear reactors.

title: Mechanism of early crack growth in carbide-free bainitic steel during impact fatigue
Sub-monolayer interface complexion to achieve significantly strength-ductility enhancement in aluminum matrix composite
Ergodicity controlled excellent transverse and shear mode piezoresponse in samarium doped PMN-xPT ceramics
abstract: Many actuation and sensing devices require piezoelectric materials with high shear and transverse mode strain coefficients. Owing to their superior performance as compared to the other state-of-the-art alternatives, this application space is largely dominated by soft PZT. In this investigation, we report excellent transverse, shear, and planar mode piezoelectric responses in samarium-doped PMN-xPT polycrystalline ceramics. In the transverse mode, the highest d31 and k31 coefficients were obtained for 2.75% Sm-doped PMN-0.28PT, with values of – 497 pC/N and 0.44, respectively. This composition also exhibited exceptional shear mode piezoelectric strain and coupling coefficients of 1020 pC/N and 0.66, respectively. The optimum planner mode coupling coefficient was 0.76 for 2.25% Sm-doped PMN-0.29PT. All these parameters exceed those of soft PZT, positioning Sm-doped PMN-xPT as an alternative for room-temperature device applications. The optimum longitudinal mode [[EQUATION]] parameter of 3.0 X 10-11 m2/N highlights the potential of 2.75% Sm-doped PMN-0.28PT as an excellent choice for energy harvesting devices. To explore the underlying mechanism for high functional response in Sm-doped PMN-xPT, the roles of contributing factors such as dielectric constant, spontaneous polarization and electrostriction were analyzed. We show that in addition to dielectric constant, the degree of ergodicity makes a subtle yet profound contribution to the piezoresponse in different modes of operation.

title: Ordered oxygen vacancies in tetragonal BiFeO3
abstract: Bismuth ferrite (BiFeO 3 , BFO) is a prototypical multiferroic material, whose crystal structures and physical properties are sensitively dependent on the strain state, forming an exotic super tetragonal phase with compressive strain. Although the compressive strain is associated with dramatically reduced oxygen vacancy formation energy, it is intuitively considered that the crystal structures of BFO are all stoichiometric. However, through multislice electron ptychography with adaptive propagator, we found that the tetragonal phase of bismuth ferrite has approximately 1/4 oxygen vacancies at the apical oxygen positions, challenging the conventional wisdom of stoichiometric BFO. Since oxygen vacancies significantly influence the physical properties of transition metal oxides, this finding offers new insights into the physicochemical behavior of bismuth ferrite and opens opportunities for the development of novel functionalities.

title: Grain-size-dependent dynamic mechanical response and plastic deformation of the FeCoCrMnNi high-entropy alloy during high-strain-rate impact
Solute-defect interaction and oxidation govern high-temperature low-cycle fatigue in Mo-added CoCrNi-based multi-principal element alloy
Crystallinity-dependent lithium storage behavior of molybdenum dioxide for lithium rechargeable batteries
Phase-field simulations of polar topologies in K0.5Na0.5NbO3 ferroelectric thin films
abstract: Polar topologies in ferroelectric materials have attracted significant attention in condensed matter physics and materials science due to their novel physical properties and immense potential for advanced ferroelectric devices. Current polar topologies are predominantly found in tetragonal or rhombohedral ferroelectrics. However, the polar topologies in orthorhombic ferroelectrics remain inadequately understood. Here, taking K0.5Na0.5NbO3 thin film as a model system, we systematically explore the possible polar topologies through manipulating misfit strain, film thickness, electric field, and electrical screening effect via phase-field simulations. We further establish phase diagrams of polar topologies, including vortices, spirals, periodic polarization waves, and skyrmions. Our results reveal that misfit strains can modulate the orientations of vortices, spirals, and periodic polarization waves, as well as the amplitudes of periodic polarization waves. Notably, a periodic in-plane electric field can reversibly switch the chirality of spirals. Moreover, tunable skyrmion density is attained via the coupling of the electrical screening effect with an external electric field. Our simulations also demonstrate the universality of Kittel's law in polar topologies. These results provide systematic theoretical guidance for discovering and manipulating polar topologies in orthorhombic ferroelectric materials, paving the way for rational design of topology-engineered ferroelectric microelectronic devices.

title: Hydrogen (deuterium) dynamics and thermal stability in ion-irradiated platinum-hydride thin films synthesized at low temperature
abstract: Hydrogen (H) and deuterium (D) interactions with transition metals are important in heterogeneous catalysis and related technologies. While H–Pt surface interactions are studied, investigations of hydrogen incorporation and transport in Pt remain limited due to its low solubility. Here, we study H(D) incorporation and desorption in metastable PtH(D) x thin films prepared by low-energy ion irradiation, enabling loading above equilibrium concentrations. Nuclear reaction analysis (NRA) reveals a nonuniform hydrogen depth profile with two accumulation regions: the subsurface and the film-substrate interface. Thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) exhibits two peaks near 190 and 230 K, consistent with hydrogen release from these regions. Resistance relaxation measurements, analyzed within a two-parallel-channel conduction model, indicate distinct kinetics for subsurface and near-interface hydrogen. For PtH x with an average hydrogen concentration of x = 0.15, Arrhenius analysis reveals two thermally activated processes, with activation energies of 130 ± 18 meV (subsurface) and 164 ± 26 meV (near interface). Above 140 K, D exhibits slower relaxation rates with activation energies of 117 ± 8 and 121 ± 7 meV for PtD x prepared under the same implantation dose. Within experimental uncertainty, the activation barriers for H and D are comparable or slightly lower for D, while the prefactors are significantly reduced for D, indicating isotope-dependent attempt frequencies and zero-point energy effects. TDS simulations based on the Polanyi-Wigner formalism reproduce the desorption spectra by resolving subsurface and near-interface contributions, consistent with the NRA profile. These findings elucidate hydrogen kinetics in PtH x relevant to Pt-based catalysis, sensing, and hydrogen–metal interactions.

title: Indium dual role in tuning ionic transport, vacancy ordering, and phase stability in SrFe1–xInxO3–δ: A concentration-dependent effect
Pressure-induced topological Lifshitz transition driven by band shift leading to enhanced superconductivity in MgSH5
Defect-mediated elemental segregation and local chemical ordering in TiZrNbTaV multi-principal element alloys
Structure and soft-mode induced phase transformation of rhombohedral phase in zirconia
abstract: ABSTRACT This work solves a long-standing ambiguity about the metastable rhombohedral (R) phase in zirconia and identifies its atomic structure and transformation pathways. Guided by X-ray diffraction (XRD)-constrained ab-initio random structure searching (AIRSS), we obtain a structural model whose Raman mode at 690 cm⁻¹ reproduces a new experimental fingerprint. In spark plasma sintered 4 mol% Y 2 O 3 -doped ZrO 2 , transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) reveal a self-accommodating lamellar microstructure (150 ± 15 nm) of alternating R and tetragonal (T) domains with a fixed orientation relationship (100) R ∥(001) T ; [01-1] R ∥[100] T . Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) O-K edges provide phase-specific spectral signatures distinguishing R from T phases. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations place R between cubic (C) and T phases in energy and show a doubly degenerate Γ-E soft mode that drives R→T phase transformation on relaxation, consistent with annealing experiments. A minimal Landau model (Γ-E order parameter coupled to in-plane shear) rationalizes stress stabilization of R and its relaxation to T or C depending on material parameters. These results newly establish the structure, spectroscopic fingerprints, and soft-mode mechanism of the R phase, informing processing-microstructure control in zirconia.

title: How glass breaks—Damage explains the difference between surface and fracture energies in amorphous silica
abstract: The relationship between free surface energy and fracture energy in amorphous silica is investigated using multiscale simulations. We combine the homogenization of an atomic scale fracture model with a phase-field approach to track and quantify the different energy contributions. Free surface energy, localized as potential energy at the surface, is clearly separated from damage diffusion extending over a 16-23 Å range around the crack path while the plastic contribution is found negligible. Analysis of the local structure reveals that diffuse damage is primarily associated with changes in the ring structure, whereas variations in free surface energy correlate with changes in the coordination number of silicon atoms. These findings provide new insight into brittle fracture mechanisms in amorphous silicates and are consistent with experimental measurements of silica toughness.

title: Shear-coupled grain growth statistics
abstract: Grain growth (GG), mediated by grain boundary (GB) migration, is a fundamental mechanism of microstructure evolution in polycrystalline materials. GB migration is frequently accompanied by a relative shear displacement of grains meeting at GBs, a phenomenon known as shear-coupling. This coupling induces internal stresses within the microstructure, which recent studies have shown to play a decisive role in dictating microstructure evolution and GG pathways. This work provides a detailed characterization of the statistical features of two-dimensional GG in the presence of GB shear-coupling through continuum modeling of GB migration that incorporates fundamental microscopic mechanisms and diffuse-interface simulations. We demonstrate that incorporating shear-coupling produces a more heterogeneous, less equiaxed microstructure than conventional curvature-driven GG, while yielding topological and geometric properties consistent with experimental and atomistic observations. We further demonstrate that as grain grows in this regime, internal stress relaxes. Highly stressed grains shrink faster, and lightly stressed grains grow faster than other grains. These findings demonstrate that internal stress, an intrinsic feature of GG, profoundly changes essential features of GG microstructure and kinetics, consistent with experiments and atomic-scale simulations. Moreover, we discuss their implications for GG regimes and scaling behavior.

title: The contribution of grain boundary complexions to the Taylor-Quinney coefficient in Cu-Zr polycrystals
abstract: During high-strain-rate plastic deformation, only part of the plastic work is dissipated as heat, quantified by the Taylor-Quinney coefficient (TQC). Although introduced nearly a century ago, the microstructural origins of TQC at high rates remain debated, with recent studies suggesting that grain boundaries (GBs) play a key role in energy storage. In this work, we quantify TQC using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Cu-Zr polycrystals, a model system that enables controlled tuning of GB composition, Zr concentration, and thickness. Cu-Zr polycrystals containing 0-3 at.% Zr were constructed and equilibrated using hybrid Monte Carlo/MD simulations to promote Zr segregation at GBs. The equilibrated cells were then sheared under adiabatic conditions, allowing simultaneous calculation of plastic work and heat generation, from which both differential and integral TQC values were extracted. The differential TQC initially ranged between 0.75 and 0.85, depending on Zr content, and increased with strain, occasionally exceeding unity. To identify the origin of the non-thermal energy fraction, we evaluated the stored dislocation energy from dislocation densities and found it insufficient to account for the discrepancy. The remaining energy was attributed to GB storage. By reconstructing GB surfaces and monitoring GB thickness during deformation, we established that GB energy density correlates with volumetric GB changes. Early-stage GB thickening accommodates a measurable portion of the non-thermal energy, while later amorphous GB transformations lead to partial energy relaxation. These results establish a direct quantitative link between GB evolution and the Taylor-Quinney coefficient in nanocrystalline Cu-Zr alloys.

title: Formation of interstitial–vacancy pairs within solute clusters of Al–Zn–Mg alloys
abstract: Vacancy-type defects introduced in water- and furnace-cooled Al–Zn–Mg alloy samples were investigated using positron annihilation spectroscopy combined with first-principles calculations. While the thermal equilibrium vacancies decreased in the sample cooled in the furnace to 373 K, vacancy-type defects were reintroduced in the sample cooled in the furnace to 303 K. This behavior is attributed to the formation of interstitial–vacancy pairs in solute clusters known as the truncated cube octahedron (TCO) shell structures. These results indicate that excess quenched-in vacancies of 10 -6 or more are not required for precipitation hardening at temperatures between 373 and 303 K. The formation of an interstitial-vacancy pair in the TCO shell structure was confirmed by first-principles-based Monte Carlo simulations starting from the solid-solution state of the Al–Zn–Mg alloy. The increase in positron lifetime observed in the furnace-cooled samples is explained by the corresponding increase in the theoretically calculated positron lifetimes associated with the formation of an interstitial Zn–vacancy pair in the TCO shell structure. Structural relaxation induced by the interstitial–vacancy pair was found to play an important role in the evolution of TCO shells into GP(I) zones.

Configuration of Schottky defects in transition metal carbides
abstract: Vacancy defects in Group 4 and 5 transition metal carbides are studied employing ab initio calculations to obtain the energies of formation of Schottky defects as well as the interaction energies for the pair of unlike vacancies in various spatial arrangements. The present calculations take into account the recently established fact that metal vacancies in these compounds may undergo a reconstruction where the octahedron of carbons surrounding the metal vacancy transforms into a lower-symmetry structure stabilized by formed C–C bonds. This reconstruction significantly lowers the formation energy of Schottky defects in cubic carbides of transition metals and also qualitatively changes the interactions between a metal vacancy and a carbon vacancy, from strong attraction to strong repulsion in the nearest-neighbor shell. The latter result shows the need to rethink the models considering clusters of unreconstructed metal vacancies with carbon vacancies in transition metal carbides. The mutual repulsion between metal and non-metal vacancies at short distances restores the usual view of a Schottky defect as a pair of dissociated vacancies in the studied equiatomic compounds.

title: Temperature dependent DC-bias effects in polycrystalline CaTiSiO5
abstract: As power devices become increasingly crucial to advanced technologies, the development of passive components, such as capacitors, has gained significant research attention. Among various candidate materials, CaTiSiO 5 stands out as a particularly promising lead-free dielectric due to its positive-bias dependence of dielectric permittivity, which originates from its antipolar structure. Although considerable efforts have been devoted to studying the effects of chemical substitutions on the crystal structure and temperature-dependent dielectric properties of CaTiSiO 5 , research on its electrical response under large electric fields remains limited, particularly regarding its behavior across wide temperature ranges relevant to practical applications. Remarkably, CaTiSiO 5 exhibits a positive DC-bias effect at room temperature, where the permittivity increases with applied electric field. This behavior is significantly different from conventional ferroelectric capacitors, arising from the coupled effects of electric field and temperature on phase structure modulation. In this work, the temperature-dependent DC-bias effect was characterized from -30°C to 150°C, where both positive and negative DC-bias effects were observed as temperature changes, providing important insight into the role of the high temperature antiferroelectric-paraelectric phase transition observed at approximately 170°C using temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy as well as small signal dielectric and elastic measurements. These data are contrasted to large-field polarization – electric field and electric-field-dependent relative permittivity measurements to more fully understand its antiferroelectric behavior and dielectric response under large electric fields, providing valuable guidance for the design of next-generation power electronic devices.

title: Strain and dopant-induced band-gap formation in metastable ZrO: resolving the experiment-simulation discrepancy
abstract: Commercial zirconium alloys form a metastable ZrO suboxide layer at the metal–oxide interface during reactor operation, yet its electronic properties remain poorly understood. Conventional PBE-DFT predicts ZrO to be metallic, in contrast to Dual-EELS measurements on corroded Zircaloy-4 that indicate a finite band gap. Here we resolve this discrepancy using a multiscale mechanical–electronic simulation approach. Bond-based peridynamics at experimentally relevant length scales was used to sample residual interface strains, which were then applied directly to atomic scale DFT models. Using higher accuracy electronic-structure methods, including the HSE06 hybrid functional and the GW approximation, we show that compressive basal-plane strain together with Sn substitutional dopants can stabilise an electronic band gap in ZrO. These results provide a mechanism consistent with experimental observations and demonstrate that strain and dopants can control gap formation in metastable transition-metal suboxides. The findings clarify the electronic nature of ZrO under reactor conditions and offer new insight into its role in the corrosion resistance of zirconium alloys.

title: Unlocking high-rate and ultra-stable sodium storage in bismuth via a catalytic-buffering intermetallic strategy

Simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility of multicomponent alloys via a synergistic study of machine learning, DFT modelling and experimental validation
abstract: In this research, we have designed, tested and optimized the compositions and properties of the Sn-Ag-Cu based multiple-component solder alloys by applying the active learning machine learning strategy and density functional theory. The active learning of adaptive iterations optimization strategy allows us to use a relatively small set of samples and much less number of experiments to achieve the alloy design goal with simultaneously increased shear strength and ductility. We discovered that Bi, In and Ni are the dominant alloying elements in controlling the trade-off between strength and ductility. Among these, Bi and In simultaneously dissolve into the Sn matrix and intermetallic compounds (IMCs) phases, synergistically improving solder joint strength through solution strengthening. Ni also plays important role in inhibiting the η → η' phase transition, producing low misfit and high-strength interfacial structures that facilitate load transfer and extrinsic toughening mechanisms via crack deflection and bridging, thereby enhancing ductility and deformation compatibility. Overall, by optimizing the alloy compositions, the newly designed alloy and the solder joints have both strength and ductility increased simultaneously with 59% higher in shear strength and 61% higher in elongation. This research has demonstrated a multi-objective optimization strategy for designing and developing multiple-component alloys, which is applicable to many other materials systems.

title: Growth twinning of the β(In) during lamellar growth of β(In) – In2Bi – γ(Sn) eutectic in rotating directional solidification: Cases with anisotropic phase boundary energy
Fingerprints of Efimov quasi-bound-state and topological phase transition in Cu2HgSnSe4 under pressure

Crystallography- and microstructure-driven design of lightweight titanium-based shape memory alloys
abstract: To facilitate the diverse functionalities of lightweight shape-memory alloys (SMAs) in various applications, it is crucial to address the research gaps in understanding and optimizing their shape-memory effects. This study presents a systematic investigation into the crystallography–microstructure–property correlations conducted on a series of lightweight TiV-based alloys. The crystallographic effect was quantitatively analyzed by tuning the lattice parameters as a function of V content. The intrinsic transformation strain was found to increase with the decreasing V concentration, reaching 7.4% along the [011] β direction while preserving a predominantly β-phase structure. However, compositional variations also influenced the phase stability and deformation mechanisms, producing distinct functional responses. Notably, the V12.5 alloy, located near the compositional threshold for the α'' martensitic transformation, exhibited a synergistic deformation mode combining the stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) and additional reorientation, achieving a recoverable strain of ∼ 9%. In contrast, alloys with higher or lower V contents primarily deformed via SIMT or reorientation alone, resulting in reduced shape recovery response. Overall, these findings provide a quantitative framework linking the variation of lattice parameters, phase stability, and deformation behaviors.

Grain boundary structure mediated heterogeneity in solute segregation and dislocation nucleation of aluminum alloys
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) are usually in a metastable state and contain various types of ledges in polycrystalline materials. The presence of these structural features may lead to heterogeneous solute segregation at nearly flat GBs in Al alloys and affect the mechanical properties of materials. In this study, the effects of GB structural features on solute segregation and dislocation nucleation are investigated by hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that local GB structural transitions and GB ledges result in the heterogeneous segregation of solutes Cu and Mg. The solute density at the GB is determined by the average segregation energy in different regions. Local structural transitions and ledges at GBs intensify strain localization, and result in a lower nucleation stress for dislocations compared to the ground-state GBs. A low concentration of the solute Cu tends to promote dislocation nucleation when it segregates at ground-state GBs, but inhibits it in other types of GBs. Conversely, the segregation of solute Mg promotes dislocation nucleation at all GBs. This difference is attributed to the effect of solute segregation on GB disorder. Increased GB disorder generates a stress gradient that provides an additional driving force for the atomic shuffling and free volume migration required for dislocation nucleation. Therefore, a negative correlation has been identified between GB disorder and dislocation nucleation stress.

title: Ni diffusion in the equiatomic CoFeMnNiV high-entropy alloy: Unexpected impact of second-phase precipitation on bulk diffusion rates
abstract: Ni diffusion in the equiatomic CoFeMnNiV high-entropy alloy is measured over an extended temperature range that covers both single-phase (face-centered cubic, FCC, solid solution) as well as two-phase (FCC solid solution + σ-phase) states. In addition, Ni diffusion experiments were performed on a single-phase σ-alloy. The σ-phase precipitation is found to affect significantly the self-diffusion kinetics in the FCC solid solution. The measured tracer diffusion coefficients follow an Arrhenius-type relationship when estimated in the single-phase solid solution, and a characteristic enhancement of the Ni diffusivity is observed at lower temperatures when the σ-phase precipitates during the diffusion annealing treatments. The enhancement is significantly suppressed when the alloy is pre-aged to approach a nearly equilibrium σ-phase volume fraction at a given temperature. Since Ni volume diffusion in the σ-phase was found to be similar to that in the FCC equiatomic counterpart, the observed diffusion enhancement is attributed to an excess vacancy concentration, generated during the growth of σ-precipitates. This excess gets eliminated when approaching thermodynamic equilibrium, i.e., when precipitation ends. A simple model of the diffusion enhancement during precipitation is proposed.

title: The origin of dislocation structures and chemical segregation in additively manufactured δ-ferritic steel microstructures
abstract: Dislocation structures generated during thermal cycling play a critical role in governing the mechanical and corrosion performance of additively manufactured (AM) alloys. While extensive studies have addressed dislocation cell formation and associated chemical segregation in face-centered cubic alloys, less attention has been paid to body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructures. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)-processed BCC alloys, dislocation densities are typically lower, solidification cell-related chemical heterogeneities minimal, and dislocation cells often absent, leaving the dislocation-related chemistries largely unexplored. Consequently, the origin of chemical segregation and the solute-dislocation interactions in LPBF-processed BCC alloys remain poorly understood. Here, a multiscale correlative microscopy approach combining plasma focused ion beam, transmission Kikuchi diffraction, scanning transmission electron microscopy, and ultrawide field-of-view atom probe tomography is employed to characterize the chemistry and crystallography of individual dislocations in LPBF-fabricated duplex stainless steels containing >98% δ-ferrite. The results reveal pronounced enrichment of N and Cr at dislocations. N segregation is attributed to elastic strain relaxation around dislocations. Density functional theory demonstrates weak and short-range Cr-N attractions, and strong and long-range Mn-N attractions, meaning Mn is stabilized in the matrix while Cr can move towards dislocations. Cr segregation levels depend on dislocation crystallography, deviating from the classical Cottrell theory. The interplay between solute drag and the thermally activated motion of BCC screw dislocations during LPBF thermal cycling influences the dislocation arrangements. These findings provide new insights into dislocation-mediated chemical heterogeneity in LPBF-processed BCC alloys and offer guidance for AM alloy design by linking LPBF parameters, dislocation evolution, and phase transformations.

Understanding creep behaviour in high performance alloys through use of the Wilshire equations
abstract: This study explores the creep behaviour of three polycrystalline alloys—stainless steel 316, Haynes 282, and Inconel 713C—chosen for their varying precipitate volume fractions. The primary aim is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms that control creep behaviour in these alloys, with a particular focus on determining the creep activation energies (Qc*) involved.SS316 displays a gradual transition in Qc* values, attributed to dislocation movement at low temperatures and twinning above yield stress at elevated conditions. Haynes 282 shows a wider range (276–427 kJ/mol), with γ′ precipitate resistance at low stress and forest hardening above yield strength. In contrast, Inconel 713C with highest volume fraction of precipitates, exhibits a constant Qc*, indicating creep governed by confined dislocation motion within γ channels, with no clear transition.The findings reinforce the application of the Wilshire equations in rationalising Qc* values and linking them to microstructural mechanisms. This provides a robust framework for predicting creep behaviour, aiding alloy development and high-temperature material optimisation.

title: Relative contributions of solutes and forest dislocations to thermally activated plasticity in hydrogen-alloyed Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic steels: analyzing stress-dependence of Haasen plot
abstract: A competitive relationship between solute atoms and forest dislocations in determining the kinetics of thermally activated plasticity was studied for a Type310S (Fe-24Cr-19Ni) austenitic steel containing ∼8500 at ppm hydrogen (H), where solute H promotes solid solution-hardening through an increase in the effective stress. The investigation was performed by constructing Haasen plot ( i.e ., strain rate sensitivity (SRS) vs. flow stress) based on stress relaxation tests, and by analyzing its evolution in relation to the decay of effective stress. In the regime of high effective stress, alloying solute elements—whose overcoming by dislocations is retarded by the presence of H—acted as primary rate-controlling obstacles to dislocations, giving rise to a relatively large and strain-independent SRS. In terms of Haasen plot , these manifested as an increase in the intercept and a decrease in the slope. Beyond the phenomenological findings of these H-induced characteristic changes, the present study elaborates their physical origin and transient nature. As the effective stress decreased and dislocation density increased, such predominance of solutes was progressively taken over by forest dislocations, leading the Haasen plot for H-charged specimens to approach that for non-charged specimen. These new insights further establish how H, alloying elements, and forest dislocations sequentially compete as rate-controlling obstacles depending on mechanical loading condition and internal state of the material.

Insights into Ni migration in long-term tested Ni-yttria stabilized zirconia electrodes by three-dimensional reconstruction aided phase-field simulations
abstract: Nickel (Ni) migration is a crucial factor in the degradation of Ni-yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) electrodes during operation. However, current hypotheses to explain the Ni migration of Ni-YSZ electrodes remain inconsistent. In this paper, three-dimensional (3D) phase-field simulations based on 3D reconstructed microstructures were utilized to understand Ni migration in long-term tested solid oxide fuel and electrolysis cells (SOFCs and SOECs). Phase-field simulations on two representative sub-volumes under open-circuit voltage (OCV) conditions revealed the impact of microstructural heterogeneity on Ni migration. Further simulations under SOEC and SOFC modes demonstrated the combined effect of this heterogeneity and contact angle gradients on Ni migration. A comparative analysis of the evolution of the microstructure, phase volume fraction, and volumetric center for two sub-volumes in OCV, SOEC, and SOFC modes revealed distinct migration behaviors depending on sub-volume size and operating mode. Ni migration was more pronounced in the small sub-volume under SOEC mode, but more significant in the large sub-volume under SOFC mode. These differences stem from the alignment or opposition of driving forces from microstructural heterogeneity and contact angle gradients. With further experimental validation, the microstructure of Ni-YSZ electrodes may be quantitatively described, even enabling lifetime predictions by integrating machine learning.

Multiscale generative inverse design for porous media via property-conditioned unit-cell assemblies: Application to VRFB electrodes
abstract: Porous materials are the reactive backbone of many technologies, especially electrochemical systems, making their inverse design a central challenge. Because microstructural features (e.g., porosity, permeability, etc.) govern fluid flow, transport, and reaction kinetics, they ultimately control component‐level and system performance from the inverse design perspective. As the utilization of additive manufacturing (AM) for porous materials continues to mature, there is a growing need for computational frameworks that co-evolve with experimental efforts and actively inform them. AI-enabled inverse design offers such a pathway: by learning meaningful latent representations that capture complex structure–property relationships, it broadens the reachable property space, helps avoid suboptimal designs, and fully exploits AM’s design freedom to manufacture high-performance materials. Building on our prior work in property-conditioned microstructure generation, we extend these tools to larger material systems by treating the material layout as an assembly of potentially 3D-printable microscale unit cells with targeted effective properties. As a case study, we leverage this proposed approach to design more energy-efficient porous electrodes to help tackle the challenges in developing vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB). More specifically, we optimize a VRFB half-cell to minimize power loss, illustrating how microstructures generated through data-driven algorithms can translate into improved porous electrode efficiency and, ultimately, lower commercialization costs for VRFBs. Although focused on VRFBs, the proposed framework is broadly applicable to other materials and engineering design problems.

title: A closed-loop multiscale computational framework for predicting barocaloric effects: Entropy decomposition and transformation mechanisms
abstract: The predictive design of metallic barocaloric materials requires a unified framework linking thermodynamics, atomistic mechanisms, and transformation kinetics. Here, we develop a closed-loop multiscale Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) framework combining quasi-harmonic thermodynamic modeling, density functional theory, and molecular dynamics simulations to enable self-consistent prediction and mechanistic understanding of barocaloric effects. Using magnesium as a representative model system, the framework quantitatively captures pressure-induced phase transitions and associated barocaloric responses with cross-scale consistency. The phase-transitional entropy change across the hcp-to-bcc transformation is dominated by vibrational contributions (~89.5%), with a secondary electronic contribution (~9.6%) associated with enhanced density of states near the Fermi energy level, while configurational effects are negligible. Atomistic simulations further reveal a shear-coupled Burgers transformation pathway linking lattice dynamics to macroscopic entropy changes. The giant barocaloric response identified near the phase boundary reflects intrinsic thermodynamic sensitivity of first-order transitions rather than practical operating conditions, highlighting the need to tune transition pressures via alloying. Based on these insights, we extract transferable design principles for metallic barocaloric materials including high lattice compressibility, dominant vibrational entropy, and favorable electronic structure features. These results establish a direct link between atomistic mechanisms and macroscopic barocaloric performance, enabling physically guided design of metallic barocaloric materials. This work provides a generalizable computational strategy for bridging multiscale modeling and materials design, offering a pathway toward the discovery of barocaloric materials with experimentally accessible operating conditions.

title: Formation of the cellular structure in the Sm2Co17-type permanent magnets: a phase-field study
Impact of oxygen and sulfur on dislocation glide in zirconium – I. Dislocation dynamics from in situ tensile tests
abstract: Sulfur addition to zirconium alloys is known to have a tremendous strengthening effect, with only a few ppm leading to a strong hardening and a noticeable decrease of the creep rate above 300 °C. Although previous works have shown an interdependent effect of oxygen and sulfur, with sulfur amplifying the strengthening of oxygen in the domain of dynamic strain aging, the physical mechanism behind this impact of sulfur addition on zirconium mechanical properties is still unknown. Using in situ straining experiments in a transmission electron microscope, we study how sulfur and oxygen modify the glide motion of dislocations for temperatures between 200 °C and 550 °C in zirconium samples with an oxygen concentration between 80 and 1300 weight ppm and a sulfur concentration up to 25 wppm. These experiments show that the velocity of gliding dislocations is reduced by the dragging of their enriched oxygen atmosphere, when the temperature is high enough for oxygen to diffuse and segregate on dislocations. Once the motion of dislocations is slowed down, segregation of sulfur on dislocations becomes also possible despite the low sulfur content, leading to a further reduction of dislocation velocity. This synergistic effect of sulfur and oxygen segregation on dislocation explains the enhancement by sulfur of oxygen strengthening in zirconium alloys.

Impact of oxygen and sulfur on dislocation glide in zirconium — II. Insights from atomistic simulations
abstract: Experimental observations during in situ tensile tests experiments have shown that a tiny amount of sulfur as low as 5 weight ppm induces a strong reduction of dislocation velocity when they interact with diffusing oxygen, amplifying the dynamic strain aging associated with oxygen in zirconium alloys above 300 °C. Using ab initio calculations, we study the interaction of sulfur and oxygen solute atoms with 〈 a 〉 dislocations in hexagonal close-packed zirconium. We show that the impact of sulfur on dislocation mobility can be rationalized by a strong short-range attraction of sulfur to the dislocation core, with attractive insertion sites existing in the stacking faults created through dissociation of 〈 a 〉 dislocations in two partials lying either in prismatic or pyramidal planes. Ab initio calculations further show that the energy barriers, which need to be overcome by sulfur atoms to reach these attractive sites, is lower than the activation energies for sulfur bulk diffusion. With sulfur diffusing faster than oxygen in zirconium, kinetics allow for sulfur segregation at temperatures where oxygen form enriched atmospheres around dislocations. This sulfur segregation in the dislocation core, which comes on top of the elastic attraction of sulfur atoms in the dislocation strain field, explains the enhancement by sulfur of the dynamic strain aging caused by oxygen in zirconium.

title: Competition and coordination of disconnection modes in shear-coupled migration of asymmetric tilt grain boundaries
Multi-scale investigation of the anisotropy of lath martensite plasticity in dual-phase steel
abstract: In Dual-Phase (DP) steel, lath martensite is generally regarded as the hard and brittle phase that determines strength and limits ductility. However, recent studies have shown that lath martensite in DP steels can also deform in a markedly ductile manner. These observations have been linked to fully lath martensitic steels, in which plasticity preferentially develops along the habit plane through several competing micromechanical mechanisms. It has remained unclear, however, to what extent these insights extend to DP steel microstructures. This paper therefore correlates the plastic anisotropy of lath martensite in DP steel to the orientation of the martensite habit plane. To this end, advanced micromechanical measurement and identification methods are applied on the same material across multiple scales, to reveal the governing deformation mechanisms and quantify statistically the influence of habit-plane orientation. Well-defined ‘1D’ and ‘2D’ tests, analyzed by microstructure-correlated strain mapping and local slip-system identification, reveal that early martensite plasticity occurs predominantly as habit-plane-aligned intra-lath slip, i.e. plasticity percolates mainly between lath boundaries. These insights are complemented by a statistical study on coarse martensite islands under realistic ‘3D’ large-strain loading, showing that strong plasticity occurs most frequently along the habit plane, even at relatively unfavorable orientations. At later deformation stages, local substructure boundary sliding is also observed. A packet-level competition analysis further indicates that IHP plasticity is approximately twice as easy to activate as out-of-habit-plane slip. Together, these results show that habit-plane-induced anisotropy is a key factor controlling the heterogeneous plasticity of martensite in DP steels.

Jahn–Teller distortion of Mn³⁺ ions as a decisive factor for the electrochemical performance of Mn substituted Na2.5-x(Fe1-yMny)1.75(SO4)3 alluaudites
abstract: Partially manganese-substituted alluaudite-type Na 2.5-x (Fe 1-y Mn y ) 1.75 (SO 4 ) 3 materials represent an attractive group of cathode materials for Na-ion batteries, offering a balance between high voltage (4 V vs. Na/Na⁺) and operational stability; however, in the case of high Mn content, it leads to a significantly reduced capacity, indicating a lack of electrochemical activity of manganese. In this study, we address the problem of explaining the lack of electrochemical activity of manganese in Na 2.5-x (Fe 1-y Mn y ) 1.75 (SO 4 ) 3 (y=1/3 and 1/2) as determined from the electronic structure calculations using the Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker with the coherent potential approximation (KKR-CPA) to account for chemical disorder. The results of both non-spin-polarized and spin-polarized KKR-CPA calculations will be discussed. Although the investigated as-synthetized Na 2.5 (Fe 1-y Mn y ) 1.75 (SO 4 ) 3 materials do not exhibit magnetic order at room temperature, information on local magnetic moments provides additional insight into the evolution of valence states during changes in chemical composition, which is essential for a better understanding of electrochemical properties. These theoretical studies will be supported by comprehensive in-situ X-ray diffraction studies, Mössbauer and X-ray absorption spectroscopies, and studies of the magnetic and electrochemical properties of the manganese-substituted iron sulfate cathode material.

Kinetics of monolayer and bilayer graphene nano-ribbon formation on 3C-SiC: Influence of substrate geometry and growth conditions
