Unraveling doping effects in LaCoO3 via machine learning-accelerated atomic simulations and active learning
abstract: Lanthanum cobaltite (LaCoO 3 ) perovskites hold promise for energy conversion, catalysis, and sensing applications, yet their performance is often limited by structural instability and moderate ionic conductivity. Strategic doping can mitigate these issues, but rational dopant design remains challenging due to the vast configurational space. In this work, we present a machine learning-accelerated framework to unravel doping effects in LaCoO 3 . Utilizing the Matlantis platform powered by universal neural network potentials, we enable efficient, near-DFT-accurate atomic simulations. The two-stage approach begins with active learning via a Bayesian neural network to distill composition–structure–energy relationships, predicting formation energy, lattice distortion, and atomic distortion across diverse A- and B-site dopants and concentrations. An artificial neural network then forward-models ionic conductivity from these properties under varying temperatures and oxygen vacancy levels. Key findings indicate that B-site doping generally stabilize the structure, while A-site doping enhances ionic conductivity by promoting structural distortions. Elevated temperatures and vacancy concentrations amplify diffusion coefficients, aligning with established transport mechanisms. To support practical applications, we developed an interactive web application, LCO-DOPER, enabling rapid dopant screening and property optimization. This framework establishes a robust foundation for data-driven design of doped perovskite materials.

title: Role of defects in the thermodynamic stability of grain boundary phases at asymmetric tilt boundaries in copper
abstract: Grain boundaries can exist as different grain boundary phases (also called complexions) with individual atomic structures. The thermodynamics of these defect phases in high-angle grain boundaries were studied mostly with atomistic and phase field computer simulations, but almost exclusively for special, symmetric boundaries. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations combined with structure search methods, as well as scanning transmission electron microscopy experiments to take a step towards understanding more general grain boundaries. Using the example of Σ 37c [ 11 1 ¯ ] tilt boundaries in Cu, we show how the grain boundary phase transition on a symmetric boundary plane is changed by the geometrically necessary defects introduced in inclined, asymmetric boundaries. We analyze the disconnections—which are dislocation-like line defects of grain boundaries—both in the simulations, as well as in experimental Cu and Al samples. A main finding is that defect energies can have a major influence on the stability of grain boundary phases, even at small inclinations. Furthermore, some defects are not able to effect large inclinations. At that point, defective asymmetric GB phases compete with grain boundaries faceting into the adjacent symmetric GB phases.

title: Entropy-regulated morphotropic phase boundary-like region in BiFeO3-based ceramics with giant electrostrain
Ferroelectricity, valley polarization, and anomalous valley Hall effect in antiferromagnetic bilayer VN2(AlO)2
PolyMicros: A foundation model for polycrystalline material structure
Cavity evolution in irradiated alloy 800H studied with in-situ ion irradiation
Direct prediction of experimental irradiation defect structures in tungsten at room temperature using stochastic cluster dynamics
abstract: The foundations of irradiation damage theory were laid in the 1950s and 60s within the framework of chemical reaction kinetics. While helpful to analyze qualitative aspects of irradiation damage, the theory contained gaps that delayed its implementation and applicability as a predictive tool. The advent of computer simulations with atomistic resolution in the 80s and 90s revealed a series of mechanisms that have proved essential to understand key aspects of irradiation damage in crystalline solids. However, we still lack a comprehensive model that can connect atomic-level defect physics with experimental measurements of quantitative features of the irradiated microstructure. In this work, we present a mesoscale model that draws from our improved understanding of irradiation damage processes collected over the last few decades, bridging knowledge gained from our most sophisticated atomistic simulations with defect kinetics taking place over time scales many orders of magnitude larger than atomic interaction times. Importantly, the model avoids any direct a posteriori fitting, and combines several essential pieces of irradiation damage physics: each playing an irreplaceable role in the context of the full model but of limited utility if considered in isolation. Crucially, we validate the model against a set of irradiation experiments specifically designed to isolate the key damage variables. Using tungsten as a model material, we find exceptionally good agreement between our numerical predictions and detailed experimental measurements of defect densities and defect cluster sizes.

title: Cellular automaton framework for non-equilibrium solidification in metal additive manufacturing
abstract: A physics-based cellular automaton (CA) model is developed to describe microstructure evolution during non-equilibrium solidification under laser additive manufacturing (AM) conditions. Unlike conventional CA approaches that assume equilibrium partitioning and lattice-dependent interface propagation, the present framework combines implicit solid–liquid interface reconstruction with a velocity-dependent partition coefficient based on the continuous growth model (CGM). The solid–liquid interface is reconstructed from a continuous solid-fraction field, while interface normals, curvature, and anisotropic growth kinetics are evaluated from spatial derivatives of the evolving solid-fraction field, reducing grid-induced growth bias commonly associated with classical CA approaches. The framework consistently couples interface kinetics, solute diffusion, curvature effects, and interfacial mass conservation within a computationally efficient CA formulation and enables quantitative prediction of dendrite tip dynamics, solute redistribution, and primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS). The model is applied to binary and ternary alloys to investigate the combined influence of growth velocity, thermal gradient, and kinetic partitioning on morphology selection and the columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET). By unifying thermodynamic consistency and kinetic effects within a CA framework, this study provides a physically grounded tool for exploring rapid solidification phenomena and microstructural selection across rapid-solidification regimes relevant to metal AM.

title: Cooling-rate effects on structural heterogeneity and the mechanical properties of aluminosilicate glasses observed over seven orders of magnitude
abstract: ABSTRACT Thermal history strongly affects structure and the mechanical properties of glasses. However, consistent experimental studies on the connection between fictive temperature, structural heterogeneity and fracture of real-world glasses remain elusive. Here, we report on a chemically homogeneous sodium aluminosilicate glass produced under cooling rates varying over seven orders of magnitude. This variation leads to a spread in fictive temperature over a range of ∼200 K; it causes distinct changes in structural heterogeneity as observed through low-frequency vibrational spectroscopy and low-temperature heat capacity studies. Independent evaluation is reported on the basis of the soft potential model (SPM), and heterogeneous elasticity theory implementing a coherent potential approximation, both providing quantifiers of structural disorder and non-affinity. Parallel analysis of mass density, elasticity, and indentation-induced plasticity and fracture allow for a direct correlation of disorder-induced changes in macroscopic material characteristics. These significantly exceed approximations obtained when considering a continuous medium transformation, underlining the foundational role of disorder and SPM percolation in macroscopic glass behavior. Our findings provide new avenues for using structural disorder as an ex ante design parameter in the conception of oxide glass materials.

title: Slip- and shuffling-based cross-slip mechanisms of c+a screw dislocations in magnesium
From bulk to surface: Structure and dynamics of amorphous alumina from deep potential molecular dynamics
abstract: Understanding the atomic-scale structure and dynamics of amorphous oxide surfaces is essential for interpreting their chemical reactivity, mechanical stability, and interfacial behavior, yet direct experimental characterization remains challenging. We employ Deep Potential (DP) molecular dynamics to generate large-scale, ab initio -quality models of amorphous Al 2 O 3 bulk glasses and melt-quenched free surfaces, enabling a quantitative analysis of both structure and relaxation dynamics with statistical confidence inaccessible to direct ab initio simulation. The trained DP model reproduces experimental liquid and glass structure, captures the cooling-rate dependence of the bulk glass transition, and corrects systematic biases in the polyhedral populations predicted by widely used classical force fields. At the free surface, mass density recovers to bulk values over ∼ 10 Å, while local coordination requires a slightly wider subsurface region to fully converge. The outermost layer is oxygen-enriched, exhibits altered polyhedral connectivity with contracted Al–O bonds, and hosts a broad population of under-coordinated motifs (notably AlO 3 and OAl 2 ) whose abundances are governed by glass stability. These under-coordinated surface motifs exhibit distinct vibrational signatures and occur as locally paired Lewis acid and Brønsted base sites consistent with bond-valence compensation, yet remain spatially dispersed rather than aggregating into extended clusters. Despite this pronounced structural heterogeneity, surface relaxation and the glass-transition temperature remain comparable to their bulk counterparts, suggesting that the disordered surface is kinetically stable once formed. Together, these results establish a molecular-level picture of amorphous alumina surfaces and demonstrate the capability of machine-learned potentials to resolve structure–property relationships in disordered oxide interfaces.

title: Route-dependent crystallization of Ni–P metallic glasses enabling a nanotwinned supersaturated Ni(P) solid solution
Interatomic potential investigation of the structural and thermodynamic properties of mixed plutonium–americium oxides
abstract: Minor actinides (MA)-bearing mixed oxides are considered for the transmutation of long-lived radioactive isotopes that result from the lifecycle and cooling of nuclear reactors. Accurate knowledge of the U – Pu – Am – Np – O thermodynamic system is necessary for the efficient and safe usage of these actinide oxides as transmutation fuel. However, experimental data is lacking for most subsystems therein, notably ternary oxides. Atomic scale calculations can be a valuable complementary tool to experiments in the production of data. The Cooper-Ruhston-Grimes (CRG) interatomic potential has proven to be a very reliable potential for simple and mixed actinide oxides, but the parametrization available in the literature yields a strongly underestimated melting temperature of PuO2. In this work, we reparametrized the CRG terms concerning Pu4+ and Pu3+ ions and obtained a potential yielding results in excellent agreement with the available experimental data. The potential was used to perform a systematical calculation of the structural and thermal properties of the (Pu, Am)O2 – x system with a Pu content from 0 to 100% and x in [0.0, 0.1] over a large range of temperatures. The results obtained with the reparametrized potential constitute important complementary data for CALPHAD models and higher-scale models describing the behaviour of nuclear fuels in operation.

title: Optimizing intrinsic strength–plasticity synergy for refractory high entropy alloy by chemical bonding engineering
Solid-state recycling of aluminum chips into high-performance crossover alloys via electroless Cu plating: Oxide elimination and doubled tensile strength
Atomic size mismatch effects on irradiation-induced defect evolution in Nb-Zr-Ti-V multi-principal element alloys
Bayesian identification of fibrous insulation thermal conductivity towards design of spacecraft thermal protection systems
abstract: The design of spacecraft thermal protection systems (TPS) requires accurate knowledge of thermal transport properties across wide ranges of temperature and pressure. For fibrous insulation, conventional measurement techniques in laboratory settings are typically limited to temperatures much lower than what is reached in atmosphere entry scenarios. Moreover, it is often the case that only temperature measurements are available, meaning that the thermal conductivity of the insulation must be indirectly inferred as an inverse problem. We propose a Bayesian framework using information field theory (IFT) to reconstruct the thermal conductivity of high-temperature fibrous insulation from sparse experimental data. Under IFT, the conductivity is represented as a Gaussian process, and the physics is enforced via a physics-informed prior over the temperature derived from the heat equation. Bayes's rule produces an infinite-dimensional posterior distribution that quantifies uncertainty about the conductivity which can be evaluated in extrapolation regimes. We apply the method to Opacified Fibrous Insulation with both synthetic and experimental data to reconstruct the thermal conductivity beyond the experimental regime. The inferred conductivities are validated against reference data and then propagated into high-fidelity digital twins of flexible TPS performance under Mars and Earth entry trajectories. The results show that IFT yields accurate predictions with quantified uncertainty, enabling robust TPS sizing in regimes inaccessible to direct measurement.

title: Dislocation-Density interactions and binary junction population formation and evolution in BCC refractory metals with random low and high angle grain-boundaries
abstract: Refractory body-centered cubic (BCC) metals, such as molybdenum (Mo), are desirable for aerospace and nuclear applications due to their thermo-mechanical behavior under extreme conditions pertaining to high temperatures and strain-rates. However, the behavior of BCC aggregates remains difficult to predict and fundamentally understand due to inherent complex and unique dislocation interactions, non-planar dislocations and cross slip, and the accumulation and annihilation of dislocation populations and densities. This study, therefore, presents a validated microstructurally based dislocation-density crystal plasticity (DCP) framework that is integrated with a nonlinear finite-element approach, to surmount the limitations of single or discrete dislocations to investigate the formation and evolution of mobile and immobile dislocation densities and dislocation junction densities in BCC molybdenum (Mo) for the formation and evolution of <001> dislocation-density junctions that are unique to BCC structures. Interaction tensors based on Frank’s energy rule are used to predict the formation of junction populations, and these predictions underscore how <001> junctions are significant obstacles to dislocation density mobility, and how they contribute to strain hardening, and evolve to junction density formation, annihilation and strain softening. A detailed examination of molybdenum aggregates with random low and high angle GB misorientations underscored significant differences in these dislocationdensity interactions and dislocation- junction density formation. This proposed framework can be used to fundamentally understand and predict large strain deformation and failure of BCC aggregates due to unique BCC dislocation-densities interactions that lead to dislocation-junction formation and evolution.

title: Machine-learning-guided molecular dynamics simulations of point defect evolution in β‑Ga2O3 during ion implantation and annealing
abstract: In beta-gallium oxide (beta-Ga2O3), Ga-ion implantation and annealing induce abundant point defects. To overcome conventional Wigner-Seitz (WS) defect analysis limitations, a defect identification algorithm based on similarity matching and DBSCAN clustering is developed for beta-Ga2O3. It distinguishes lattice atoms from defects at high concentrations and identifies eight Ga interstitial configurations (Gaia to Gaih). Comparing SRIM and MD data highlights electronic stopping effects: neglecting them overestimates ion range and defect concentration. Across five fluences (1 to 5 x 10^14 cm-2), 1373 K is the optimal recovery temperature. Multiscale analyses using hydrostatic stress, PRDF, and defect concentration reveal defect evolution. Ga interstitials (Gai) occupy tetrahedral and octahedral sites, driving a defect-mediated phase transition from beta- to gamma-Ga2O3. Increasing fluences reduce beta-phase recovery and increase gamma-phase transformation irreversibly. Oxygen interstitial (Oi) migration is sensitive to annealing temperature, which enhances O-sublattice recrystallization.

title: Predicting co-segregation in alloys with solute-solute interactions
abstract: The co-segregation of impurities in systems with multiple solute species has been widely recognized as an effective strategy for tailoring material properties. However, reliable predictions of co-segregation behavior remain a significant challenge for alloy design in these systems. In this work, we develop an extended dual-solute (DS) segregation framework to semi-quantitatively predict co-segregation behavior with solute-solute interactions, including both homoatomic and heteroatomic contributions. A machine-learning workflow is first established to predict the pairwise segregation energy to construct the DS segregation energy spectra that intrinsically include both types of solute-solute interactions. The resulting spectral information is then used to determine the upper and lower bounds of segregation for individual solute species. When applied to magnesium-based ternary systems constructed by alloying Mg with any two of the 11 candidate solute species (Ag, Al, Ca, Co, Cu, Gd, Nd, Ni, Pb, Pd, and Zn), the extended DS segregation framework is successfully validated by hybrid molecular dynamics/Monte Carlo simulations and experimental results available in the literature. Furthermore, we introduce a design strategy to promote co-segregation by incorporating additional solute species that exhibit attractive interactions with existing solutes, thereby enabling enhanced co-segregation even in the presence of strong site competition. These results underscore the critical role of solute-solute interactions in governing co-segregation behavior and provide a predictive pathway for the design and optimization of alloys.

title: Revealing the shock-induced complex phase transformations of tin and their impacts on spallation
Junction-governed diffusion kinetics and nanovoid formation in three-dimensional grain boundary networks
abstract: In polycrystals, grain boundaries (GBs) are widely accepted as potential diffusion pathways and crack-initiation sites. GBs always form network structures in three-dimensional (3D) materials including regular GB planes, triple junctions (TJs), and high-order junctions (HJs), and thus the influence of these components on the mechanical behavior of polycrystals should be understood. In this study, we used molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with a new on-the-fly GB component identification method to investigate dynamic behaviors such as atomic diffusion and nanovoid formation under uniaxial tensile loading in body-centered cubic (bcc)-Fe polycrystals. Our results show that the local atomic diffusion ability of the HJ is the highest among the GB components, followed by those of the TJ and GB. Uniaxial tensile loading simulation results suggest that junction-rich regions containing multiple HJs and TJs act as hotspots for nanovoid formation. Stress concentration at HJs provides the driving force for vacancy/nanovoid formation, and high atomic diffusivities of TJs and HJs facilitate vacancy transport and aggregation. The obtained results for the atomic diffusion ability and nanovoid formation of the GB components are comparable to previous experimental observations. The present study contributes to a deeper, fundamental understanding of the mechanical behavior of 3D GB networks and highlights the GB network topology as an important factor in controlling the mechanical properties of nanopolycrystals.

title: Physics-informed process-structure-property prediction model for additively manufactured metallic parts
A dual-scale chemical fluctuation nanostructure enables CoCrFeNiPd high entropy alloy with exceptional mechanical properties at ultralow temperatures
Room-temperature plastic deformation of single crystals of Mg17Al12 with the body-centered cubic α-Mn (A12) type structure
abstract: The deformation behavior of single crystals of Mg 17 Al 12 has been investigated by micropillar compression at room temperature as a function of crystal orientation and specimen size. Three slip systems, {110}<111>, {110}<001> and {110}<110>, are identified to operate in crystal orientations in the middle of the stereographic triangle, close to [ 1 ‾ 11] and [001], respectively. The latter two slip systems are identified in the present study for the first time. The averaged CRSS values obtained for micropillar specimens in the size range of 1.5 to 10.6 μm do not vary significantly with slip system, and they are 295, 325, and 300 MPa for {110}<111>, {110}<001>, and {110}<110> slip, respectively. While the specimen size dependence of yield stress is negligibly small for {110}<001> and {110}<110> slip, that for {110}<111> is comparatively large. The bulk CRSS values estimated by the extrapolation of the size-dependent yield stress are 200±35, 305±50, and 280±55 MPa for {110}<111>, {110}<001>, and {110}<110> slip, respectively. As predicted by DFT (density functional theory) calculations, there are some stacking faults of sufficiently low energy, leading to two- and three-fold dissociation for the dislocation with b (Burgers vector)=1/2<111> carrying {110}<111> slip and the dislocation with b=[110] carrying {110}<110> slip, respectively. The deformation behavior of Mg 17 Al 12 is compared to that of isostructural α-Mn, in particular, in terms of the existence of low-energy stacking faults and the resultant dislocation core dissociation/spreading.

title: Emerging relaxor behavior induced by quenched random fields in Bi1/2K1/2TiO3‒Bi1/2Li1/2TiO3 solid solutions with cation vacancies
abstract: Bi 1/2 K 1/2 TiO 3 (BKT)-based solid solutions are promising lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics for electromechanical and energy storage applications. In this study, we investigate the structural, dielectric, and polarization properties of the ceramics of Bi 1/2 K 1/2 TiO 3 ‒Bi 1/2 Li 1/2 TiO 3 solid solutions [Bi (1+ δ )/2 K (1− x )(1−3 δ )/2 Li x (1−3 δ )/2 V δ TiO 3, BKT‒BLT] containing A-site vacancy ( V ) to elucidate the impacts of the Li + substitution for K + and the introduction of A-site vacancies on relaxor behavior. The temperature dependence of relative permittivity reveals that, upon cooling, the characteristic behavior of BKT, i.e., the temperature ( T )-induced spontaneous relaxor-to-ferroelectric phase transition, disappears in BKT‒BLT. Moreover, the E -induced irreversible relaxor-to-ferroelectric phase transition is hampered by increasing the contents of Li + ( x ) and A-site vacancies ( δ ). Interestingly, even a small amount of A-site vacancies can effectively reduce the freezing temperature ( T f ) and stabilize the ergodic relaxor phase with dynamic polar nanoregions (PNRs). The reduction of T f becomes more significant under the coexistence of Li + ions and A-site vacancies due to the simultaneous introduction of quenched random stress and electric fields arising from local structural distortions and local charge imbalances. As a result, BKT‒BLT exhibits slim P - E hysteresis loops with enhanced maximum polarization ( P max ), suppressed remanent polarization ( P r ), and superior energy storage properties compared with BKT. These findings establish a strategy for designing high-performance lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics by engineering quenched random fields in the BKT-based perovskites for energy storage applications.

title: Laser powder bed fusion of a newly designed Fe-based bulk metallic glass with enhanced soft magnetic properties
abstract: Additive manufacturing of Fe-based bulk metallic glasses (BMGs) is hindered by their limited glass-forming ability (GFA) and by devitrification during repeated thermal cycling in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), which degrades soft magnetic performance. Here, we investigate the LPBF processability of a newly designed Fe–Si–B–Nb–Ni alloy exhibiting enhanced GFA (critical casting thickness ≈1 mm) without the addition of P, Co, or rare-earth elements. A systematic study combining varied energy densities, time delays, and double-scanning strategies is conducted to establish processing–structure–property relationships. Multiscale characterization (X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry, electron backscatter diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, atom probe tomography, and X-ray computed tomography) reveals that the improved GFA suppresses micron-scale crystallization across a broad processing window, yielding amorphous fractions above 87% and fully XRD-amorphous states under optimized remelting conditions. Atom probe tomography confirms chemical randomness irrespective of scan strategy, whereas calorimetry and nanoindentation mapping demonstrate that double scanning reduces structural heterogeneity through enhanced relaxation of the amorphous phase. This relaxation increases resistance to devitrification during subsequent thermal cycles. The resulting as-built specimens exhibit coercivities as low as 44 A m⁻¹, i.e. over an order of magnitude lower than previously reported for P-, Co-, and rare-earth-free Fe-based MGs processed by LPBF, while maintaining stable specific saturation magnetization. At high amorphous fractions, coercivity becomes weakly correlated with residual crystallinity and more sensitive to porosity and structural heterogeneity. These results demonstrate that synergistic alloy and scan-strategy design can control structural relaxation and crystallization pathways in LPBF-processed MGs, providing a mechanistic foundation for manufacturing high-performance soft magnetic components.

title: Experimental Measurement of Polycrystalline-Average Grain Boundary Segregation using X-Ray Diffraction
Field inhomogeneous distributions and local percolations in Ag-BaTiO3 ceramic-metal composites: The role of microstructural variability
abstract: This work investigates how composition and microstructural variability influence the dielectric properties of xAg–(1–x)BaTiO 3 ceramic-metal composites (denoted as CerMet) through combined modelling/experimental approach. Virtually generated microstructures predict different percolation ranges depending on microstructural modifications. To check such effect, a range of compositions with x ≤ 20 vol.% were synthesized using single-step or two-steps sintering to ensure compositional integrity and similar BaTiO 3 grain size. During the consolidation, Ag undergoes melting, migration, and infiltration, generating intricate metal–ceramic connectivity. The permittivity exhibits percolation-like increases near critical compositions around ∼5, ∼11.5, and >20 vol.%, reaching a maximum value of εᵣ ≈ 17,000 at 20°C with tan δ ≤ 2% (at 10 kHz) for x = 11.5 vol.%. The high permittivity compositions selected for X-Ray tomography and detailed microscopic analyses revealed 3D microstructures with specific features, where field concentration (“hot spots”) occurs. These results demonstrate how metal melting during sintering governs microstructural evolution and variability and the important role of the elongated and tortuous filler structures in increasing the CerMet effective permittivity towards giant values towards the percolation limits.

title: Helium-mediated dislocation loop rafting in tungsten
Robust out-of-plane ferroelectricity in Aurivillius ultrathin films through local chemical antisite
A general synthesis strategy for volatile-element-based compounds: Achieving near-zero thermal expansion and advanced microwave absorption in Yb2Fe17 and its nitride
abstract: The synthesis of ytterbium (Yb)-based intermetallic compounds via conventional physical methods has been substantially hindered by the pronounced volatility of ytterbium, impeding both fundamental magnetic studies and practical implementations. This study develops an in-situ confined reduction-diffusion (IC-RD) strategy coupled with compaction-encapsulation technology, effectively mitigating the evaporation of ytterbium. This method successfully yields high-purity Yb2Fe17, which is subsequently converted into Yb2Fe17N3-δ via nitridation. Neutron powder diffraction (NPD) analysis reveals a near-zero thermal expansion (near-ZTE) behavior in Yb2Fe17, characterized by an ultralow volumetric thermal expansion coefficient (αv) of 1.6 × 10-⁷ K-¹ within the 100-250 K temperature range. Furthermore, nitriding significantly enhances the magnetic properties, leading to a higher magnetic ordering temperature and large saturation magnetization in Yb2Fe17N3-δ. When incorporated into a paraffin composite, Yb2Fe17N3-δ exhibits outstanding microwave absorption performance, achieving a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of -50.5 dB at 3.37 GHz in the S-band (2-4 GHz), along with a maximum effective absorption bandwidth (EABmax) of 5.96 GHz at a minimal thickness of 1.4 mm. This study not only establishes a viable synthetic pathway for compounds containing highly volatile elements, but also opens avenues for designing materials with tailored structural and magnetic properties, as well as advancing thin-layer broadband microwave absorbers.

title: Refractory high-entropy alloy films with synergistic effect of suppressing interfacial interdiffusion and modulating surface electronic structure
Plasticity enhancement via β-relaxation modulation in metallic glasses: Energy engineering
Interstitial carbon tuning of low-angle grain boundary and dislocation activity in a bulk near-α titanium for ultrahigh ductility
Influence of SiO2 addition on the voltage stability of PTCR ceramics
abstract: The rise of E-mobility leads to intensive research into power electronics. Increasing onboard voltages of 800 V to 1200 V pose a challenge to electrical components like PTCR thermistors, which are applied as self-regulating heating elements, current limiters, or temperature sensors in battery electric vehicles (BEV). PTCR materials are characterized by a positive temperature coefficient of resistance (PTCR). However, the PTCR effect is limited by the breakdown field strength E BD at which PTCR materials lose their self-regulating ability. A critical factor to enhance the E BD of PTCR ceramics is the addition of a flux such as SiO 2 . In this study, the effects of the SiO 2 addition on the potential barrier and microstructure are discussed and their influence on voltage stability is evaluated assuming the validity of the Heywang-Jonker model. We developed an estimate for the average grain size with the volume weighted d V 50 and proofed its feasibility as an estimate for the average grain size along the conduction path in the Heywang-Jonker model. However, while we present a ceramic with a maximum E BD of 1118 V·mm -1 at w SiO 2 = 0.9%, we show that for w SiO 2 > 0.9% the practical voltage stability in form of the E BD is decoupled from the assumptions made by the Heywang-Jonker model. We prove that the deterioration of the E BD for w SiO 2 > 0.9% contradicting our results for the Heywang-Jonker model is founded in the destabilizing field enhancing effect of increased inhomogeneities in the ceramics.

title: Core-shell-matrix heterostructures enable high strength and ductility of titanium alloys
Hydrogen effects on the cyclic creep deformation mechanisms of 310s austenitic stainless steel
abstract: Hydrogen effects on cyclic plasticity of austenitic stainless steels represent a critical issue for fatigue design, as constitutive behavior is essential to assess both global and local mechanical responses of structures. In this work, the effect of solute hydrogen on cyclic hardening and cyclic creep deformation of AISI 310S, uncharged and hydrogen-charged (∼113 wppm), was investigated prior to crack initiation. To elucidate hydrogen–plasticity interactions under cyclic loading, a consistent mechanical database covering a range of mean stress σ m and maximum stress σ max levels was established under stress-controlled tension-compression ratcheting at 300 K (0.05 Hz) and compared with static creep. Internal stresses were quantified by partitioning the flow stress into back stress X and effective stress σ eff , and dislocation structures were characterized by quantitative TEM. The tensile plastic strain history, governed by σ max , reveals three deformation regimes, each distinctly affected by hydrogen. In Regime 0 (low σ max ), hydrogen promotes planar slip and homogeneous dislocation distributions, yielding high plastic strain reversibility and suppression of cyclic creep. Consistent with reduced stacking fault energy and inhibited cross slip, hydrogen increases the threshold stress σ th for the onset of cyclic creep. In Regime I (σ max > σ th ), the cyclic creep rate follows ln(dε r /dt) ≈ K(σ max /μ) + B, where μ is the shear modulus; hydrogen decreases the slope K, attributed to enhanced plastic strain reversibility and delayed formation of polarized dislocation walls. In Regime II (high σ max ), well-developed dislocation cell structures dominate, and the influence of hydrogen becomes less pronounced. Across Regimes I and II, the cyclic creep rate scales uniquely with the back-stress amplitude X a , independent of hydrogen content, indicating that fluctuations of long-range internal stresses govern ratcheting. This finding reflects the ability of cyclic loading to progressively destabilize the dislocation structure; hydrogen mitigates this effect primarily through enhanced short-range pinning.

title: Extending stable potential window by multi-principal element passivation in complex alloys
In-situ formation of nanoscale Hf dispersoids enabling exceptional strength-ductility synergy and superior thermal stability in Mo alloys
Combination of ultra-high strength, enhanced thermal conductivity, and large negative thermal expansion in La(Fe, Si)13 alloys via in-situ forming multi-phase
Intra-regional strain partitioning within initial austenite regions in medium Mn steels
High-energy {134¯1} twin boundaries and hierarchical twinning behavior in a near-α titanium alloy under biaxial loading
Probing the role of 3D intergranular interactions in local subcoercive switching of textured piezoelectric ceramics
abstract: The electromechanical responses of individual grains embedded in ferroelectric ceramics are modulated by local boundary conditions imposed by neighboring grains. In this work, in situ far-field high-energy X-ray diffraction microscopy data were collected for a strongly textured manganese-doped lead-magnesium-niobate-lead-zirconate-titanate ceramic manufactured by templated grain growth. Domain variant volume fractions were estimated for hundreds of grains before and after applying a subcoercive electric field and combined with spatial information to correlate local subcoercive switching behavior with grain neighborhood characteristics. Subcoercive switching was associated with the extent to which a grain's as-poled domain state deviates from that of a perfectly-aligned single crystal, likely reflecting contributions from local features that cannot be resolved with this technique (porosity, grain boundary phases, local composition variations). Competition was observed between grain orientation and intergranular interactions, with the former observed to be less important than the latter when grain volumes were considered. Larger misorientations within the tape-casting plane and reduced ferroelastic switching among near-neighbors were associated with reduced subcoercive switching, together implying a coordinated intergranular switching mechanism. Collectively, these findings emphasize the role of intergranular interactions in modulating local electromechanical response, offering insights into factors responsible for deviations in textured ceramic response relative to single crystals.

title: Segregation-induced structural reconfiguration and chemically actuated migration of grain boundaries in multi-principal element alloys
Precipitates suppress the deformation-induced phase transformation in FCC-phase multi-principal element alloys
Editorial Board
Opportunities and challenges of megahertz X-ray synchrotron radiography for in situ materials science applications due to high dose rate
abstract: Characterising ultra-high-speed dynamic events in the bulk of the material requires high-frame-rate imaging, combined with X-rays capable of penetrating the material. Megahertz radiography with synchrotron radiation was explored, showing strong potential for capturing dynamic damage events. In situ tensile tests were performed on fibre-reinforced polymer composites to image transverse crack dynamics. Challenges of this experimental technique were highlighted and complemented with plausible strategies. The first challenge stemmed from the limited buffer capacity of the high-speed camera, which was addressed by designing two triggering strategies based on electrical conductivity and load drops. The second challenge concerned dose effects due to the high photon flux required for ultra-high-speed radiography, which led to a degradation of the specimen by thermal effects. Dose calculations were performed, and a heat transfer model was developed to quantify the dose rate effect. Increasing beam energy and enhancing cooling were proposed to mitigate the heat load, providing actionable insights for future ultra-high-speed radiography experiments across a wide range of applications.

title: Elevated rolling contact fatigue resistance of gradient dislocation structured martensitic bearing steel
Large magnetovolume effect in multifunctional ferromagnet MnSb driven by unconventional magnetostructural coupling
abstract: Magnetostructural coupling plays a crucial role in numerous types of quantum materials and functional magnetic materials. Here, we investigate the magnetostructurally active ferromagnet MnSb, whose derivative compounds Mn 1 + x Sb are strong candidates for magnetocaloric applications. We reveal an unusually large spontaneous magnetostriction effect in MnSb, resulting in a relative unit cell expansion of up to 1% and an extended temperature region of negative thermal expansion of the crystallographic a axis. This magnetovolume effect is exceptional not only because of its magnitude, but also because the volume increase begins in the paramagnetic phase and exhibits unconventional linear scaling with the short-range ferromagnetic correlations as the temperature is lowered, before switching to quadratic scaling with the long-range-ordered magnetic moment below the transition. We explain this exceptional behavior through unusual trilinear couplings among the lattice strain and domains of distinct magnetic order parameters. Heat capacity measurements also provide new thermodynamic information about MnSb, including determination of the Debye and Einstein temperatures to be 164 and 296 K, respectively. These findings greatly expand our understanding of MnSb and provide insights into the fundamental materials physics of magnetostructural coupling in the presence of short-range magnetic correlations, with potential for broad applicability.

title: Crystallographic transformation of UO2 to U4O9, U3O7, and U3O8
abstract: The oxidation of UO 2 plays a critical role in the performance and long-term behaviour of nuclear fuel, yet the crystallographic nature of the intermediate uranium oxides and the mechanism of their formation remains poorly understood due to their complex structures and the lack of suitable single-crystal samples. In this work we investigate the oxidation of epitaxial [ 0 0 1 ] UO 2 thin films using in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction, enabling direct observation of structural evolution throughout oxidation. We show that oxidation proceeds topotactically from UO 2 to U 4 O 9 , U 3 O 7 , and U 3 O 8 , with the U 4 O 9 and U 3 O 7 phases forming as multi-domain single crystals. Comparison with calculated reciprocal space maps identifies the U 4 O 9 structure as the β phase, while the U 3 O 7 phase exhibits complex domain behaviour and additional superstructure reflections indicate a lower symmetry than that in present structural models. The final transformation to U 3 O 8 is accompanied by a large volume expansion and pronounced loss of crystalline coherence, although a clear topotactic relationship between ( 0 0 1 ) UO 2 and ( 1 3 0 ) U 3 O 8 is retained. The identification of these topotactic relationships allow us to build a mechanistic understanding of the transformations between phases. These results provide insight into the structural mechanisms governing the oxidation and spallation of UO 2 and establish a route to accessing single-crystal U 4 O 9 and U 3 O 7 via controlled oxidation.

title: Leveraging the polymorphic phase transition for high piezoelectricity in barium titanate-based lead-free piezoceramics
High-performance Fe-based superalloys designed via large language models and knowledge graphs

UNi4Mn: A non-centrosymmetric uranium intermetallic exhibiting room-temperature ferromagnetism
abstract: We report UNi 4 Mn, a non-centrosymmetric uranium intermetallic exhibiting room-temperature ferromagnetism with a Curie temperature (T C ) of 336 K. This behavior arises from localized Mn 2+ moments and enhanced 5 f -3 d hybridization. Differential thermal analysis indicates congruent formation at 1185 °C. The compound crystallizes in the cubic MgCu 4 Sn-type structure (Pearson symbol cF 24, space group F- 43 m ) with Mn atoms fully ordered on the 4 c site, as determined by X-ray and neutron diffraction. Magnetization measurements yield an effective magnetic moment (μ eff ) of 5.6 μ B per formula unit and a saturation magnetic moment (μ sat ) of 4.85 μ B per formula unit, consistent with localized Mn 2+ behavior. Neutron diffraction reveals magnetic moments only on the Mn sites, while U and Ni atoms remain nonmagnetic; Mn moments order ferromagnetically and align along the cubic face diagonal. Density functional theory calculations reproduce the ferromagnetic ground state of UNi 4 Mn and its Ce analogue CeNi 4 Mn, and confirm the Pauli-paramagnetic character of UNi 5 . The calculations further show that enhanced 5 f -3 d hybridization strengthens exchange interactions, leading to Dirac-like electronic features and a pseudogap at the Fermi level, with potential implications for spintronic and quantum devices. To our knowledge, UNi 4 Mn represents the first uranium-based intermetallic combining room-temperature ferromagnetism with non-centrosymmetric symmetry, providing mechanistic insight into how chemical ordering, hybridization, and local coordination govern magnetic exchange in actinide intermetallics.

title: Isothermal annealing effects on β-relaxations and crystallization behaviors in amorphous GeTe
abstract: A secondary (β) relaxation process is the dominant source of atomic dynamics below T g in many glass forming systems. Recent studies reported the presence of β-relaxations in amorphous phase-change materials (PCMs). They showed that suppressing β-relaxation via annealing in Ge 15 Sb 85 can effectively slow down its crystallization kinetics. Yet, when Sb is replaced by Te, a similar annealing protocol has little effect on the Te-rich alloy Ge 15 Te 85 , which is a good glass former. Here, we investigate amorphous GeTe that is a Sb-free PCM, but with faster crystallization kinetics than Ge 15 Te 85 . GeTe is a typical PCM, i.e., crystallizes very rapidly. Using powder mechanical dynamic spectroscopy, we observe a clear reduction of the excess-wing in the loss modulus upon isothermal annealing of amorphous GeTe, indicating a suppression of its β-relaxation. Combining ultrafast calorimetric analysis and time-resolved optical reflectivity measurements shows that, whereas as-deposited GeTe exhibits stochastic crystallization behavior, annealed samples crystallize more slowly but also with reduced stochasticity. Synchrotron X-ray scattering experiments reveal increased Peierls-like distortions in the amorphous structure after annealing, and demonstrate that, even if annealing introduces nucleation sites, it nonetheless slows down crystallization kinetics. These finding suggests that, in the annealed GeTe, crystallization is limited by crystal growth rate, which is retarded through a process likely associated with the suppression of β-relaxation.

Impact of interstitial carbon on local lattice distortions in CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys
abstract: Here, we explore component-dependent local lattice distortions in polycrystalline, equiatomic, face-centered cubic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys and their modifications induced by dilute interstitial carbon. Multi-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy combined with reverse Monte Carlo analysis reveals that the Cr component experiences the most substantial local distortions, independent of the temperature of prolonged annealing treatments (993 K or 1373 K) and the nominal carbon content (0 to 0.8 at.%). The static disorder around Cr atoms was found to increase markedly and monotonically upon carbon alloying, whereas Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni demonstrate weaker and non-monotonic tendencies. The carbon-induced lattice distortions extend over several coordination shells, indicating the early stages of carbide-related local configurations specifically around Cr absorbers. First-principles density functional theory and finite-temperature molecular dynamics simulations confirm the preferential occupation of Cr-rich interstitial sites by dilute carbon. These results provide decisive hints towards the atomistic origin of the non-monotonic diffusion behavior previously reported for carbon-doped CrMnFeCoNi alloys, and are noticeable for understanding the carbon-induced phase transitions in compositionally complex systems.

title: Solid oxide cells degradation by Nickel oxidation: A phase field study of oxide growth and its mechanical impact
abstract: Solid Oxide Cells are highly efficient energy conversion devices that can be damaged by various system failures. Specifically, the porous hydrogen electrode, which is a cermet consisting of Nickel and Yttria Stabilized Zirconia (Ni-YSZ), can deteriorate when exposed to oxidizing atmosphere at high temperature. Ni oxidation induces volumetric expansion which is partially accommodated in the pores of the cermet. This constrained swelling imposes mechanical strain on the YSZ backbone that can compromise its integrity. In this study, a conventional cermet was oxidized under air at 700◦C for different times to characterize the kinetics and features of Ni oxidation and the fracture of YSZ. A novel tri-material phase-field model, incorporating oxidation-induced strains, was developed to simulate Ni oxidation within the complex electrode microstructure. The model was validated on different cermet microstructures to reproduce the kinetics of oxidation in the different electrode layers and the YSZ mechanical loading after oxidation. The material parameters governing oxidation (Ni diffusion in NiO) and stress state (oxide growth strain) were identified through the model calibration. A correlation between oxidation and microstructural features was identified, revealing that Ni coarsening slows oxidation kinetics, and enabling pre-simulation DoO estimation with a microstructure descriptor. Simulations revealed localized high tensile stresses at several YSZ necks, matching experimental crack initiation timescales and validating a first step towards oxidation-induced damage prediction.

Secondary twinning and twin–twin interaction mechanisms of {112¯1} deformation twins in rhenium
abstract: Deformation twinning plays a central role in the plasticity of hexagonal close-packed (hcp) metals, and twin–twin interactions together with secondary twinning can strongly influence their mechanical response. Yet these phenomena remain insufficiently understood, especially for the less common { 11 2 ¯ 1 } extension twins. This study investigates these mechanisms in single-crystal rhenium using in-situ transmission Kikuchi diffraction tensile testing along the [0001] axis. We observe two distinct secondary twinning phenomena. First, native secondary twins form abundantly within primary twins, independent of twin interaction sites. Their nucleation is rationalized by their high Schmid factor and the energetically favorable dissociation of basal dislocations at primary twin boundaries. Second, specific twin-twin interactions trigger a distinct secondary variant selection producing a crossing-like morphology. While these twin crossing configurations violate classical geometric criteria, we show that variant selection is governed by the local stress state and plausibly facilitated by the dissociation of non-basal dislocations. These findings establish a stress- and dislocation-based framework for secondary twinning in { 11 2 ¯ 1 } extension twins, offering new insights into deformation anisotropy of hcp metals.

Defect Energy Formalism for CALPHAD thermodynamics of dilute point defects applied to intrinsic point defects in Mg2Si
abstract: Accurate prediction of point defect thermodynamics is essential for controlling material functionalities. In semiconductors and insulators, even dilute defects can govern carrier transport, recombination, and ionic conductivity, thereby influencing the performance of thermoelectric, photovoltaic, and solid-state ionic devices. While first-principles methods can determine defect energetics, their integration with macroscopic thermodynamic frameworks such as CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) remains limited. This gap has led to empirical CALPHAD models in which Gibbs energy parameters are fitted to available data, restricting predictive capability, especially for semiconductors with dilute defects where thermochemical, non-stoichiometry, and phase-fraction measurements are scarce.We recently introduced the Defect Energy Formalism (DEF), a first-principles-based, dilute-limit adaptation of the compound energy formalism (CEF) for modeling point defects within CALPHAD, eliminating the need for adjustable empirical parameters. Here, we apply DEF to interstitial, antisite, and vacancy defects in anti-fluorite Mg2Si and examine the resulting thermodynamic stability and properties of non-stoichiometric Mg2Si. We outline a general procedure for extracting and calibrating first-principles defect energetics from the literature, reconciling reference energy conventions between DFT and CALPHAD, and integrating them into the CALPHAD-DEF framework. This enables the direct construction of DEF models for any material–defect system from existing first-principles and bulk thermodynamic data. Finally, we demonstrate DEF’s flexibility by progressively increasing model complexity by adding competing defects and defect-induced entropy effects to assess their impact on defect concentrations, validate predictions against standard Arrhenius-type predictions, and discuss defect behavior under non-equilibrium conditions shaped by kinetic barriers or synthesis constraints.

title: Complex He diffusion pathways induced by elemental diversity in refractory high entropy alloy MoNbTaVW
abstract: The performance of plasma-facing components in nuclear fusion reactors is limited by radiation-induced degradation, particularly helium accumulation and transport. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown enhanced irradiation tolerance, yet the physical origin remains debated. We argue that conventional barrier-based models cannot fully explain helium cavity growth and migration observed in HEAs. Therefore, we explore a new framework for studying helium diffusion by investigating its pathways in a body-centered cubic refractory HEA (MoNbTaVW), a medium-entropy alloy (MoNbTa), and reference Ta, using ion implantation, isochronal annealing, transmission electron microscopy, elastic recoil detection analysis, and atomistic simulations. We show that increased elemental diversity leads to increased tortuosity of helium diffusion pathways, yielding persistent local mobility but strongly reduced long-range net displacement. Atomistic simulations reveal that helium preferentially probes local potential-well volumes associated with elements of lower local valence-electron density (V, Nb, Ta), resulting in highly tortuous trajectories characterized by short step lengths and frequent directional changes. This pathway-level confinement explains the experimentally observed coexistence of large local helium cavities and limited long-range transport in the damage-peak region. These results provide a trajectory-based perspective for understanding diffusion in HEAs under irradiation.

Atomic-scale solute redistribution during high fluence neutron irradiation of a zirconium cladding alloy
abstract: In this study we have used a combination of atom probe tomography and (scanning) transmission electron microscopy to investigate solute redistribution under high fluence neutron irradiation in a Zr-Nb-Sn-Cu-Fe experimental fuel cladding alloy. The bulk samples were exposed to neutron irradiation in the BOR-60 reactor up to 33.5 dpa. By mapping solute distributions and quantifying solute compositions in carefully defined regions of irradiated materials, we show that during irradiation Fe and Cu are gradually depleted from second phase precipitates, grain boundaries and interfaces present in the unirradiated state, forming characteristic bands of enrichment at arrays of microstructural defects on the basal plane. In-solution Sn and Nb concentrations in the unirradiated material are depleted to form Sn bands that are spatially out-of-phase with Fe and Cu bands, and Nb clusters which agglomerate and coarsen with longer irradiation exposure. The compositions of both the original β-Nb second phase precipitates and the irradiation-induced Nb clusters converge on ~Zr-35%Nb after heavy irradiation. These results provide new insights into solute redistribution during irradiation. The significant microchemical variations observed at high doses can be used to refine mechanistic understanding of the coupled irradiation and corrosion processes of cladding under in-reactor conditions.

title: Hierarchical defect coupling leading to glass-like phonon thermal conductivity and infrared spectrum shielding in cation-deficient Nd(2-2x)/3CaxTiO3
Sluggish recrystallization in additive manufactured stainless steels explained with in-situ EBSD
abstract: Additive manufactured alloys exhibit sluggish recrystallization kinetics compared to their conventionally processed counterparts, requiring higher homologous temperatures and extended annealing times to achieve full recrystallization. The metallurgical mechanisms advanced so far include front pinning by second-phases (oxides or other particles) or solute drag. We collect multi-scale and time-resolved in-situ EBSD to capture recrystallization in directed energy deposited 304L stainless steel at 950 ° C. By fitting classical kinetics models and the microstructural path method to these unique datasets, we reveal that recrystallization is characterized by early but sparse nucleation and early grain impingement. The recrystallization front is particularly tortuous and advances with intermittent, stop-and-go motion. After excluding particle pinning and solute drag effects by means of complementary ex-situ annealing and thermodynamics modeling (diffusion and dissolution), we show that the dislocation cell networks inherited from rapid solidification and thermal cycling pin the recrystallization front. This leads to intermittent front motion governed by the topology of the dislocation cell networks. These findings suggest that post-build heat treatments should be designed not only to overcome stored strain energy barriers but also to disrupt or progressively relax the thermally stable dislocation-cell network inherited from additive manufacturing. More broadly, the mechanism is expected to be relevant to other low- to medium-stacking-fault-energy FCC alloys that develop persistent cellular dislocation structures during processing.

title: Phase field crystal modeling of subgrain coarsening
abstract: Recovery of plastically deformed metals involves several stages of substructure evolution during which dislocation entanglements and networks become increasingly organized, thereby lowering the stored energy in the material. Central to recovery is the formation and evolution of subgrains, which is also recognized as a recrystallization precursor. In this paper, subgrain coarsening is investigated by means of phase field crystal (PFC) simulations. PFC enables tracking subgrain evolution with atom-scale spatial resolution and over extended time scales, beyond the reach of alternative methods such as molecular dynamics simulations. Different subgrain models are devised to investigate various relevant conditions for subgrain coarsening, both with and without the presence of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs). The results show that subgrain coarsening initially takes place by sub-boundary dissolution and rearrangement. At later stages, the coarsening is dominated by subgrain boundary migration—somewhat similar to normal grain growth—but with instances of subgrain coalescence. Lattice rotation within the subgrain network is demonstrated to occur gradually under the formation of intra-subgrain orientation gradients. The results also reveal that a presence of HAGBs is not a prerequisite for subgrain coarsening, even if involving coalescence, contrary to the classical assumption. Subgrain coarsening is, in fact, shown to proceed more efficiently without any HAGB influence in all of the investigated scenarios.

title: A spectral-model analysis of grain boundary segregation in Cu-Ni alloys: roles of enthalpy, entropy, and statistical coupling
abstract: Understanding grain-boundary segregation in Cu–Ni alloys has been hindered by conflicting reports: dilute-limit radiotracer experiments suggest pronounced segregation, whereas atomistic simulations and indirect measurements often indicate little to no segregation. Here, we combine EBSD-based boundary identification with atom probe tomography to directly quantify grain-boundary chemistry in a Cu–9 at% Ni alloy. No measurable Ni enrichment is observed at any boundary type or annealing temperature, providing a firm experimental benchmark for concentrated Cu–Ni alloys. To reconcile these findings with dilute-limit measurements, we employ a spectral model that captures the full distribution of segregation energies and its statistical reshaping under varying global compositions. The model shows that, in the ultra-dilute limit, segregation behavior is strongly influenced by the lowest-energy portion of the spectrum, leading to enhanced segregation at low temperatures. The trends of the model are consistent with those observed in radiotracer experiments, though these experiments still show much more boundary enrichment than expected purely thermodynamically. In contrast, at bulk-relevant compositions, solutes occupy a broader range of boundary sites, and the net segregation factor approaches unity. Using both bivariate joint distributions and a generalized Gaussian copula formulation, we further demonstrate that segregation behavior is primarily governed by the structure of the enthalpy spectrum, while entropic contributions and enthalpy–entropy coupling play a secondary role and do not significantly alter the predicted trends.

title: Redox thermodynamics and hydrogen production of ferrite-based multi-cation oxides for thermochemical water splitting

Defect physics and iron substitution in tremolite: A first-principles study of a complex silicate
abstract: Complex silicate minerals exhibit chemically diverse and structurally intricate frameworks, yet the mechanisms governing their defect formation and defect-mediated properties remain poorly understood. Here, using first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate intrinsic point defect formation and Fe substitution in tremolite, a representative Ca–Mg amphibole. We find a pronounced sublattice dependence of defect formation: framework cation vacancies are energetically costly and weakly site-dependent, whereas oxygen vacancies are strongly site-sensitive and become thermodynamically accessible under p -type conditions. A central finding is that charge compensation universally governs defect stabilization, dictating distinct electrostatic pathways for intrinsic versus extrinsic defects. While intrinsic antisite defects are stabilized through donor–acceptor pairing with native oxygen vacancies, extrinsic Fe dopants trigger a reversed compensation logic, pairing preferentially with native acceptors to form highly stable neutral defect clusters. Crucially, the activation of these extrinsic compensation pathways is governed by local hydration and redox conditions. This environment-dependent pathway selection controls the Fe 2 + / Fe 3 + ratio, providing an atomic-scale origin for the intervalence charge transfer and systematic color variations (from pale green to dark brown) observed in natural amphiboles. More broadly, these results establish charge compensation as a unifying principle for defect formation in complex silicates and demonstrate that transition-metal doping via intrinsic compensation networks is a more effective approach for property tuning than the manipulation of isolated intrinsic defects.

title: Decoupling 2H and 3R polymorphs in A5B19 La–Mg–Ni-based superlattice hydrogen storage alloys for enhanced cycling stability
Atmosphere-dependence and mechanistic origin of preparation-induced martensite transformation in 17-4 PH stainless steel fabricated by laser powder bed fusion
abstract: This work resolves the observed atmosphere dependence on phase constitution in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of high-nitrogen 17-4 PH stainless steel (EOS GP1) and identifies the mechanism responsible for previously reported discrepancies. The results demonstrate that both nitrogen and argon atmospheres yield a nearly fully austenitic structure under optimal processing parameters. Microstructural differences, previously attributed to processing atmosphere, are demonstrated to arise not from processing itself, but from atmosphere-dependent susceptibility to preparation-induced martensitic transformation (PIMT). Characteristic features of PIMT-formed martensite are summarized to facilitate its recognition. A mechanistic framework is established to explain this atmosphere-dependent behavior by linking melt pool geometry, thermal history, residual stress heterogeneity to PIMT susceptibility. Finally, a distinct PIMT mechanism governed by the chemical composition is proposed, based on a review of prior studies on high-nitrogen 17-4 PH steels. Together, these findings reconcile contradictory reports in the literature and highlight the necessity of depth-resolved, multi-technique characterization when interpreting microstructures in metastable austenitic alloys processed by LPBF.

title: Dual-orientation growth enabling multiple stable interfaces in directionally solidified Gd2Zr2O7/GdAlO3 eutectic ceramics
Systematic investigation of composition–microstructure–property relationships in the HCP Ti-Zr-Hf model system
abstract: Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP) alloys are used in structural materials applications for extreme environments such as those involving cryogenic conditions, or for nuclear cladding. However, the alloy design space explored for HCP compositionally complex alloys, namely High-Entropy or Medium-Entropy Alloys (hereafter referred to as HEAs) has been limited. Here, we propose the Ti-Zr-Hf ternary system as an ideal model for developing single-phase HCP HEAs and systematically investigate its composition-microstructure-property relationships. CALPHAD thermodynamic calculations predicted, and experimental results confirmed, that a stable single-phase HCP solid solution forms over a wide compositional range. The as-cast microstructure exhibited a systematic evolution dictated primarily by Hf content: high-Hf content alloys formed coarse dendritic structures via diffusion-dominant transformations, whereas low-Hf alloys formed fine acicular structures through diffusionless martensitic transformations. This change with Hf content is rationalized by a compositional dependence of the Continuous Cooling Transformation (CCT) kinetics. Nanoindentation revealed a strong solid-solution strengthening effect, with hardness generally increasing from 4.3 GPa in Ti-rich compositions to 5.5 GPa in high Hf-content alloys. Notably, the equiatomic TiZrHf alloy demonstrated an exceptional synergy of high yield strength (1140 MPa) and superior ductility (elongation >16%). Post-deformation analysis revealed that this is governed by the Twinning-Induced Plasticity (TWIP) effect, via the activation of {10-12} extension twins, confirmed by a characteristic misorientation angle of ∼86° across twin boundaries. Comparing alloys of contrasting c/a ratio at fixed Ti content further revealed a transition from twinning- and stacking-fault-mediated plasticity to confined planar slip, consistent with the reduced {10-12} twinning shear and enhanced slip accessibility that accompany a higher c/a ratio; the as-cast morphology, by contrast, modulates the magnitude of the work-hardening response rather than the operative deformation mode. This work establishes the Ti-Zr-Hf system as a cornerstone for developing high-performance HCP HEAs.

title: Modeling the impact of twin boundaries on the deformation of nanotwinned metals: A dislocation dynamics approach
Simultaneous control of phase stability and crystallographic texture for low-modulus biomedical β-type Ti–Cr–Al alloys by in-situ-alloying LPBF
abstract: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) offers not only geometric freedom, but also a unique route to co-design composition-based phase stability and crystallographic texture, which are critical for realizing low-modulus Ti alloys. In this study, we fabricated Ti–Cr and Ti–Cr–Al alloys by the in situ alloying of elemental powders and programmed single-crystal-like textures (<100>, <110>, or <111> // build direction (BD)) via tailored scanning strategies. By employing processing conditions that yielded a melt pool depth far greater than the layer thickness, compositionally uniform builds were achieved through multiple remelting events. In Ti–12Cr (mass%), which has relatively low β-phase stability, the ω phase was observed despite not being detected in its solution-treated-and-quenched counterpart. This observation suggests that the LPBF-specific thermo-mechanical history, including a tensile residual stress of 353 MPa, may have contributed to ω-phase formation. The addition of Al suppressed the formation of ω, resulting in a single-phase β matrix. Furthermore, scan-strategy-dependent textures were consistently observed across all the compositions. The elastic modulus showed pronounced orientation-dependent anisotropy, reaching ∼60 GPa along <100> in a Ti–12Cr–3Al composition, whereas the BD-parallel yield strength approached 800–1,000 MPa depending on the texture, producing elastic admissible strains that surpass those of reported LPBF-fabricated Ti–6Al–4V. Based on these findings, we propose an additive manufacturing process-aware design framework in which alloy composition, LPBF-specific thermo-mechanical history, and crystallographic texture contribute collectively to phase stability and directional mechanical properties in metastable β-Ti alloys.
