An experimentally informed model of meso‑scale architecture of CeO2 hierarchical catalyst: the role of structural hierarchy of Ru-decorated Co-doped CeO2 in propane oxidation
abstract: In this study original approach for modeling of the mesoscale architecture of hierarchical catalyst has been presented. Data from TEM, HRTEM, SEM, SAED, and ET were used to inform the construction of model of texture of hierarchically structured CeO2 particle via crystallographic modelling approach. The model allowed to explain the exceptional activity of Ru/CeO2 hierarchically structured catalyst (T50= 130°C, Ea = 33 kJ/mol), and its enhanced self-regenerative action. While the architecture of CeO2 catalyst is imprinted in the crystallographic structure of the Ce(HCOO)3 catalyst precursor, the driving principle for texture formation is geometric fitting of ceria crystallites along the directions of similarity of structural motifs of both materials. Structural elements dissimilarity is behind formation of channels that allow rapid diffusion of gaseous thermolysis products that leads to development of highly porous catalyst that exposes (110) CeO2 facets inside the porous volume, which poses compromise between activity and stability. Doping hierarchical ceria by cobalt ions changes the architecture and increases activity of the catalyst but decline of activity is seen when specific texture is lost for highly doped samples. Structural hierarchy facilitates self-regenerative property of Ru-decorated CeO2 system due to fostering redispersion of Ru inside the porous volume of macroparticle during variable conditions of catalytic process. The presented approach for synthesis and modelling of hierarchically structured oxides opens possibility of knowledgeable design of materials showing synergistic properties.

title: Tailoring tensile properties of Al88Ni10MM2 metallic glass by in-situ precipitation of FCC-Al nanocrystals under controlled cooling rates
abstract: Amorphous alloys offer unique opportunities for tailoring microstructures via non-equilibrium processing; however, precise control of nanoscale crystallization during rapid solidification remains challenging without post-solidification heat treatments. Herein, we demonstrate that in-situ precipitation of FCC-Al nanocrystals in an Al 88 Ni 10 MM 2 (MM: Ce-rich misch metal) metallic glass can be effectively controlled solely by tuning the cooling rate during melt-spinning. By systematically varying the wheel speed from 40 m/s to 10 m/s, corresponding to cooling rates from 2.5 × 10⁶ K/s to 4.0 × 10⁵ K/s, we achieve a substantial increase in the number density of FCC-Al nanoprecipitates from 2.15 × 10²¹ to 1.55 × 10²² m⁻³, while maintaining a nearly constant nanocrystal size (∼5–6 nm). To elucidate the governing nucleation kinetics, nucleation delay times were quantified using flash differential scanning calorimetry and employed to construct Time-Temperature-Transformation and Continuous-Cooling-Transformation diagrams. Statistical analysis of nucleation temperatures enables direct estimation of nucleation rates under different cooling conditions, revealing that reduced cooling rates significantly enhance nucleation kinetics, leading to dense in-situ precipitation. In contrast, crystal growth remains strongly diffusion-limited under rapid solidification conditions, thereby constraining precipitate coarsening. Consequently, we establish a cooling-rate-dependent framework for decoupling nucleation and growth during melt-spinning, enabling high-density nanocrystal formation without significant size evolution. Mechanical testing, including ribbon bending and cyclic tensile experiments, confirms that such controlled in-situ nanocrystallization simultaneously enhances both tensile strength and plasticity, addressing one of the long-standing challenges in metallic glass research. This work provides a processing strategy for cooling-driven microstructural design in metallic glasses, offering a pathway to bypass conventional annealing treatments while achieving enhanced mechanical performance.

title: Covariant formula for the driving force for interface migration
abstract: Interfaces of crystalline materials are strongly affected by the anisotropy of interface energy. A key quantity in this context is the interface stiffness tensor, which characterizes the response of the interface energy to changes in interface orientation and plays a role in determining the driving force for interface migration. The latter is expressible via contraction of the stiffness tensor and interface curvature tensor. Practical computations involving tensors necessarily rely on their individual components. In this work, an explicit component-wise expression is derived for the contraction of the stiffness and curvature tensors, valid in arbitrary coordinate systems. Within this formulation, to get the driving force, the curvature tensor is contracted with the pullback of a stiffness-related tensor – originally defined in three-dimensional Euclidean space – onto the interface manifold. This covariant treatment establishes a physically consistent foundation for three-dimensional computational models involving interface stiffness.

title: Anisotropic deformation behavior of LPBF fabricated Co35Cr25Mn15Ni15Fe10 with low stacking fault energy studied by in situ neutron diffraction
Quantitative characterisation of γ′ precipitation and its role in governing robust properties in the Alloy 925 material system
abstract: This work quantitatively investigates the γ′ precipitation behaviour and mechanical properties of the Alloy 925 (UNS N09925) material system to elucidate its resilience to compositional variations and aging treatments. Using advanced characterisation techniques, it is shown that both composition and aging parameters have a distinct influence on the volume fraction and size of γ′ precipitates during production-relevant heat treatments, including one-step aging at 720–760°C and subsequent second aging steps at 621–635°C. Quantitative analysis of the γ′ volume fraction, implementing a novel analysis procedure for high-energy X-ray diffraction data proposed in this work, shows that minor changes to the Ti and Al contents result in changes of up to 2 vol.% in the γ′ phase during aging. In addition, the introduction of a second aging step at lower temperatures increases the γ′ fraction by approximately 2.5 vol.%. Small-angle X-ray scattering captures not only the progressive coarsening with increasing temperature and time during one- and two-step aging, resulting in precipitate diameters ranging from 4 to 22 nm, but also the compositional effect on precipitate size. The experimentally obtained quantitative data for the γ′ precipitates allow the prediction of the yield strength increase associated with precipitation strengthening as well as the validation of precipitation kinetics modelling. Comparison with the results of hardness measurements reveals a strong correlation between the γ′ precipitation behaviour and the mechanical properties due to order-type strengthening associated with the weakly coupled dislocations mechanism.

title: Tailoring ionic conductivity in argyrodite-type solid electrolytes via simultaneous P5+/Sn4+ and S2-/I- substitutions
Planar antisite defect-engineered domain structures in BiFeO3 thin films
High crack propagation resistance of polysynthetic twinned TiAl single crystals induced by delamination cracks
abstract: Polysynthetic twinned (PST) TiAl single crystals exhibit exceptional potential for application in aero-engine blades, making the investigation of their fracture behavior highly essential. Here, the crack propagation behaviors and fracture mechanisms of PST TiAl single crystals are systematically investigated from room temperature to 900 ℃ for the first time. The results show that fracture toughness exhibits significant orientation dependence: 0°-Type II＞0°-Type I＞45°＞90°. For 0°-Type II specimens, the improved fracture resistance is primarily attributed to the activation of delamination toughening. Delamination toughening associated with cracking at γ/α2 interfaces normal to the primary fracture surface, which dramatically improves overall fracture resistance. During delamination, numerous new interfaces are created that consume energy. This effectively increases the energy release rate and contributes to the exceptional fracture toughness. Meanwhile, the TWIP effect makes the deformation of the lamellar bundles more uniform, preventing rapid fracture from local necking, and enhancing the resistance to crack propagation. In 0°-Type I specimens, the lamellar interface hinders crack growth, causing the path to deflect repeatedly. Additionally, the TWIP effect appears at the crack tip, blunting it and increasing the crack propagation resistance. For the 45° specimens, the crack propagation mode transitions from Mode I to a mixed Mode I/II. The crack shifts from the divider direction to propagate along the lamellar plane, leading to relatively low crack propagation resistance. In 90° specimens, the crack plane is parallel to the lamellar planes, allowing cracks to propagate rapidly and resulting in the weakest crack-propagation resistance.

title: Concentration-dependent suppression of thermal anisotropy in 4H-SiC by nitrogen doping
Self-pinning and Self-climbing of skyrmion dislocations through topological characterization: Lattice mechanics of deformable quasiparticles
abstract: Skyrmions are emergent quasiparticles in ferromagnets possessing topologically identified unique dynamics, stability, and deformability. They self-assemble into skyrmion lattices whose collective behaviors are central to both fundamental understandings and spintronics applications. However, in contrast to atomic crystals, the lattice mechanics in skyrmion lattices, where lattice defect dynamics mediate macroscopic deformations, remain elusive. Here, we revealed unconventional defect dynamics in skyrmion lattices, including self-pinning and self-climbing of dislocations accompanied by large skyrmion deformations with topologically protected transitions from a single skyrmion to half-skyrmions. Our phase-field simulations demonstrate that external field dependent skyrmion deformability fundamentally alters lattice defect behaviors from conventional atom-like dislocation glide to the phenomena unique to topological quasiparticles. These behaviors are successfully revealed by topological characterization and described by strain analysis. This study not only provides critical insight into spintronics engineering for skyrmion-based devices but also establishes a foundation for a new class of mechanics, “quasiparticle lattice mechanics”.

title: Integrated molecular dynamics modelling of the full electron beam physical vapor deposition process chain in nickel thin films
abstract: ABSTRACT Electron Beam Physical Vapor Deposition (EB-PVD) is a critical technique for high-performance coatings, but modeling its full non-equilibrium process chain, i.e., from source evaporation to film evolution, remains a significant challenge. This study presents a comprehensive, integrated Molecular Dynamics (MD) framework that simulates the entire non-equilibrium EB-PVD process for nickel thin films, in which vapor composition, atomic configuration, velocity, incidence angle, and atomic flux obtained from open-boundary evaporation are directly transferred to the deposition model. The emitted vapor is predominantly monomeric, while larger clusters form during subsequent gas-phase transport. Vapor density primarily governs collision and aggregation, whereas vapor temperature controls cluster coarsening and persistence. During deposition, film morphology shifts from cluster-size controlled to substrate-controlled regimes: roughness increases with cluster size on smooth surfaces while this sensitivity is substantially reduced on rough substrates. This work provides critical atomic-level predictive insights for microstructural engineering and performance optimization in EB-PVD systems.

title: Insights into the mechanism of kink band formation: Case study on an additively manufactured BCC Ti-9V-3.5Al-5Sn-3Zr-2.5Mo-0.2O alloy
Ferroelectric domain-wall dynamics in point-defects elastic fields: A phase-field study
Stress partitioning, variant selection, and anisotropic elastic response during martensitic transformation in Fe–Ni–C alloy under constant tensile stress
Modelling thermal expansion of pure metals and steels
Irradiation-driven recrystallization in fusion-grade tungsten: A mesoscale, microstructure-aware model
Double-peak age strengthening of magnetostriction in heterogeneous Fe-Ga alloy
High-temperature EBSD reveals the link between ferroelastic switching, martensitic transformation, and lattice correspondences in zirconia ceramics
Beyond averaging: δH, a chemical heterogeneity descriptor for single-phase formation prediction in multicomponent alloys
abstract: A new dimensionless descriptor for single-phase microstructure prediction in multicomponent alloys (MCA) and high-entropy alloys (HEA) is proposed: the normalised dispersion of binary mixing enthalpies, δ H . This descriptor quantifies the internal heterogeneity of chemical interactions among constituent element pairs —a contribution that classical descriptors do not capture, as they rely on weighted averages that mask the coexistence of strongly attractive and repulsive pairs. Combined with the atomic size mismatch parameter δ , the pair δ H – δ significantly outperforms the Ω – δ reference criterion established by Yang and Zhang (2012), with an improvement of +3.16 percentage points in cross-validated accuracy (83.16% vs 80.00%) and +0.063 in the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (0.663 vs 0.600), validated on an experimental dataset of 1675 alloys from three independent sources spanning binary to nonary compositions (McNemar test, p = 0.006). Although δ H and δ are moderately correlated at the global level (Spearman ρ = 0.27), partly because both tend to increase with compositional complexity, the significant improvement of δ H – δ over any univariate classifier confirms that δ H contributes predictive information that δ alone does not capture. The critical threshold δ H ≤ 1.1 has a direct physical interpretation: the solid solution is stable when the heterogeneity of binary chemical interactions does not exceed 1.1 times the mean thermal energy available at the solidification temperature.

title: Corrigendum to “Intra-regional strain partitioning within initial austenite regions in medium Mn steels” [Acta Materialia 319 (2026) 122658]
Effect of Al on microstructural evolution and hot corrosion behavior of AlxCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy coatings fabricated using laser directed energy deposition
Why does Re anti-segregate from the grain boundaries in Ni?
abstract: Abstract In virtually every polycrystalline material with more than one elemental constituent, grain boundaries (GBs) offer preferential sites for minority elements to occupy; the phenomenon of GB segregation is ubiquitous. Here, in stark contrast, we report a rare observation of “antisegregation” in a clean binary alloy of Ni-Re. In addition to being unusual, this observation also runs counter to prior density functional theory predictions, which suggest that rhenium should segregate to GBs in Ni. From first principles, we demonstrate that this discrepancy originates from a magnetic effect. Whereas the zero-Kelvin calculations that are typical for assessing GB segregation energies are appropriate for the low-temperature, ferromagnetic state of Ni, GB segregation is a high temperature phenomenon where the system is paramagnetic instead. This magnetic change turns out to flip the sign of the segregation tendency on average, and indeed predicts GB solvent enrichment, rather than typical solute enrichment. With a multiscale, quantum-accurate model, we apply machine learning methods to address the full, complex case of a polycrystalline system. The analysis shows that when this magnetic effect is accounted for, the experimental antisegregation is quantitatively predicted with accuracy. Our findings call for a broader focus on magnetic disorder as a critical factor in GB segregation science and high-temperature alloy design.

title: Pressure-induced local structural heterogeneity in a metallic glass
Development of a Zr-based bulk metallic glass with excellent industrial producibility and high fracture toughness
Grain boundary stability dictates the rate-limiting deformation process in nanocrystalline metals
abstract: Nanocrystalline metals can exhibit both dislocation-mediated and grain boundary (GB)-mediated plasticity, making it difficult to identify the rate-controlling unit process. Here, we vary GB structural stability in Ni- and Pt-based films through deposition route and alloying, and determine the governing deformation mechanisms by coupling transient activation-parameter measurements with simultaneous in situ transmission electron microscopy observations. Despite having comparable mean grain sizes, the films with different nonequilibrium GB states separate into two reproducible mechanical regimes. In the grain-coarsening regime, rapid stress-assisted grain growth influences the plastic flow rate, and the measured activation volume is small (∼4-5 b ³ in Ni and 3-4 b ³ in Pt). In the stable-grain regime, the plastic flow rate is controlled primarily by dislocation activity, and the measured activation volume is larger (∼7-12 b ³ in Ni and 6-10 b 3 in Pt 90 Au 10 ). The measured activation volumes for the stable-grain condition agree quantitatively with atomistic predictions for GB dislocation nucleation, whereas the smaller values measured during grain coarsening are attributed to diffusion-assisted GB motion. These results show that, in addition to grain size, GB structural stability is a key variable influencing which localized process controls plastic flow in nanocrystalline face-centered cubic metals.

title: Revealing the effects of dealloying on hydrogen evolution reaction catalysis by distribution of relaxation times analysis
Frank-type stacking faults in 4H-SiC: A unified crystallographic, thermodynamic, electronic, and optical framework
abstract: Frank-type stacking faults (FSFs) are among the most important extended defects in 4H-SiC, yet their crystallographic classification, transformation mechanisms, electronic structures, and optical properties remain incompletely understood. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation of FSFs in 4H-SiC through the integration of high-angle annular dark-field high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF HR-STEM), photoluminescence (PL) mapping and spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. By rigorously applying Frank’s original crystallographic definition, we resolve long-standing ambiguities in the intrinsic/extrinsic classification of FSFs and demonstrate that the widely discussed (3,2) FSF is intrinsically classified despite involving an insertion-mediated formation process. Direct atomic-scale observations further reveal structural connectivity among the standard (5,2), (4,2), and (4,1) FSFs, providing experimental support for one possible crystallographic evolution pathway linking these faults. Investigations of non-standard FSFs show that identical Zhdanov notations can correspond to either intrinsic or extrinsic fault configurations depending on their crystallographic topology. DFT calculations establish, for the first time, comprehensive stacking-fault energies and electronic band structures for both standard and non-standard FSFs. While most FSFs exhibit conventional 3C-like quantum-well states, the (1,1) and (2,1) FSFs display distinct 2H-like electronic characteristics associated with dominant K-point split-off states. Finally, direct HR-STEM/PL correlation and first-principles calculations identify the characteristic PL emission wavelength of the standard (4,1) FSF as 459 nm, demonstrating that the long-accepted 424 nm assignment is inconsistent with both experimental and theoretical evidence. These results establish a unified crystallographic, thermodynamic, electronic, and optical framework for FSFs in 4H-SiC.

title: The thermodynamic and crystallographic origins of hysteresis in NiTi–Nb shape memory alloys
abstract: Achieving wide thermal hysteresis in NiTi-based shape memory alloys is critical for coupling and sealing applications. Yet, the physical mechanisms governing this behaviour in NiTi–Nb remain disputed, which has limited the application of predictive design principles to wide-hysteresis alloys. In this study, a systematic series of NiTi–Nb alloys were investigated using differential scanning calorimetry and in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction to separate the effects of microstructure and crystallography. Crucially, this study demonstrates that the characteristic hysteresis widening is not driven by the presence of β -Nb phase. Instead, a synergistic thermodynamic mechanism is identified, whereby Nb additions decouple the transformation temperature from crystallographic compatibility. Unlike binary NiTi, where lowering the transformation temperature naturally improves compatibility, Nb additions maintain a large lattice incompatibility even as the martensite start temperature is suppressed to low levels. At these low temperatures, the transformation entropy is intrinsically low; consequently, the system requires a significantly larger undercooling to generate the necessary driving force to overcome the strain energy barrier, resulting in a larger thermal hysteresis width. Additionally, Nb was found to enhance phase homogeneity and suppress intermediate R-phase formation. These findings provide a new, physically grounded criterion for the design of wide-hysteresis shape memory alloys.

title: High-throughput screening of oxidation kinetics in a combinatorial library of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr(-Al)-based superalloys
Multiscale insights into the important roles of grain orientation and boundary in hydrogen embrittlement of a Ni-based bicrystal superalloy
Cryogenic plasticity enhancement of additively manufactured refractory high-entropy alloys via dislocation junctions
abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are promising for structural applications in extreme environments. However, their cryogenic deployment has been fundamentally constrained by reduced plasticity that results from insufficient dislocation multiplication and severe strain localization. Here, we report an additively manufactured (AMed) Nb40Ta25Ti15Hf15Zr5 RHEA produced via in-situ multi-metal alloying laser-directed energy deposition (LDED) without any post-processing. This alloy exhibits a fracture elongation of 20.5 ± 0.4 % at -196 °C, representing a 3% improvement over its conventionally recrystallized counterpart. It is found that the complex thermal cycling of AM introduces high-density dislocations and multijunctions within the alloy. These pre-existing dislocation configurations create an inherent multi-slip environment and lower the energy barrier for forming multijunction networks under the low activity of screw dislocations at cryogenic temperatures. From the initial stage of deformation at -196 °C, the multijunction networks form throughout the matrix, acting as dynamic sources for dislocation multiplication via debris-mediated mechanisms and enabling sustained planar slip, which significantly enhances the cryogenic deformability of the alloy. This work presents a cost-effective pathway for designing AMed RHEAs with exceptional cryogenic strength-ductility synergy, paving the way for next-generation structural materials tailored for extreme environments.

title: Strength retention induced by thermally stable nanoprecipitates in an additively manufactured Al-Fe-Cr-Sc-Zr alloy after long-term exposure at 400 °C
Defect-mediated mechanisms of deformation-induced martensitic phase transformations in structural alloys: application to austenitic stainless steel
abstract: Deformation-induced martensitic transformations are a common feature of workhorse and advanced structural alloys, such as 300-series austenitic stainless steels, transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) steels, and emerging high-entropy alloys. Despite many decades of study, the fundamental mechanisms by which these transformations proceed have been elusive. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations combined with line defect analysis to reveal the mechanisms underlying two exemplar martensitic transformations in a 300-series-like steel: a reversion transformation from HCP ε-martensite to FCC γ-austenite and a transformation into BCC α’-austenite. Both transformations were observed to occur at twin and ε-martensite slip band intersections, in agreement with microscopy observations reported in the literature. Contrary to prevailing theories, we found that both transformations proceeded via nucleation and expansion of line defect loops (partial dislocations and disconnections) in the primary slip band. Using atomistic analysis tools, the precise Burgers vectors and line defect morphologies responsible for the transformation were characterized and correlated with nucleation and propagation of the martensitic phases. Our findings provide a pathway towards predictive models of martensitic transformations useful for alloy design and engineering predictions.

title: Achieving a superior combination of ambient and high-temperature mechanical properties in a precipitation-enhanced α+β Ti alloy via cluster-formula design
Structural and chemical length scales at near-stationary austenite-ferrite interfaces in a model duplex stainless steel
abstract: The structural and chemical properties of austenite/ferrite (γ/α) interfaces were investigated in a model duplex stainless steel (Fe–Cr–Ni–Mo–N) using a correlative approach combining scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and atom probe tomography (APT). Two interface types were selected based on their orientation relationship (OR): a near-Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) interface and a non-K-S interface. The near K-S interface presents a planar terrace-ledge morphology with atomically sharp structural transitions at the terraces, whereas the non-K-S interface is rough with protrusions of 3–5 nm amplitude. In both cases, the chemical transition width measured by EELS and APT exceeds the crystallographic interface width determined from STEM imaging, indicating that chemical potential perturbations extend beyond the structural discontinuity. The OR is found to have a clear effect on the solute segregation behavior: Mo and N segregate exclusively to the non-K-S interface, while Cr segregates to both interface types. Ni shows no detectable interfacial excess at either interface. The 2D APT composition maps reveal a spatially heterogeneous distribution of Cr at the near K-S interface, with a strong spatial correlation between Cr and N enrichment attributed to their attractive thermodynamic interaction. Gibbsian interfacial excess values and segregation energies are reported for all solutes, distinguishing between effective and intrinsic contributions. Thermodynamic self-consistency of the derived segregation energies is only achieved for an interface width of 1–2 nm, consistent with the chemical width from EELS. This provides an experimentally grounded estimate of the interface width directly applicable to solute drag models of γ/α interface migration.

title: Atomic-scale interface kinetics during non-equilibrium solid-vapor phase transition in crystalline metals
Resolving the metastable Si-XIII structure through convergent theory and experiment
abstract: Silicon allotropes have emerged as a pivotal frontier for engineering materials with tailored optical, electronic, and thermal functionalities, opening routes toward integrated photonics, energy harvesting, and quantum technologies, while avoiding rare or toxic elements. High-pressure experiments have revealed several metastable silicon allotropes, among which Si-XIII stands out. First observed more than 20 years ago, this phase has remained structurally unidentified, representing a significant gap in our understanding of elemental silicon allotropy. In this work, a convergent methodology is employed combining advanced theoretical modeling with experimental characterization to finally resolve the long-standing structural assignment of Si-XIII. We construct a structural model guided by experimental observations, validate it through first-principles optimization, and systematically test it against multiple experimental signatures. All key fingerprints of this phase — interplanar spacings, Raman frequencies, thermodynamic stability, and kinetic pathways — are consistently rationalized by our proposed crystal structure. These findings provide a crucial missing piece in the high-pressure phase diagram of silicon, demonstrate the power of integrating computational predictions with experimental validation to resolve complex structural problems in materials science, and open new avenues for the controlled synthesis and functional exploitation of metastable Group-IV allotropes.

title: Toughening of additively manufactured NiAl-28Cr-6Mo nanostructured composites by modification of the local microstructure
abstract: NiAl-(Cr,Mo) in-situ composites such as NiAl-28Cr-6Mo (at.%) exhibit a high fracture toughness due to their directionally solidified two-phase microstructure. The reinforcing (Cr,Mo)-phase hinders the crack propagation through the brittle B2-NiAl-matrix. In this study, two different morphologies with a range of achievable phase thicknesses in a NiAl-28Cr-6Mo alloy are produced by additive manufacturing. This resulted in either an isotropic, interconnected rod network or a lamellar microstructure. Due to the small size of the phases, the fracture properties of the so formed nanostructured composites are analysed locally by focused ion beam (FIB) milled microcantilevers. It was shown for the first time that an isotropic, interconnected network exhibits a maximum fracture toughness of 9 MPa√m at a (Cr,Mo)-phase thickness of 50–70 nm. In contrast, the fracture toughness of the plate morphology (6–8 MPa√m) is largely independent of the (Cr,Mo)-phase thickness. However, (Cr,Mo)-plates with a favorable crack arrester orientation demonstrate significantly higher work of fracture due to active toughening mechanisms during extended stable crack growth, compared to the rod-network morphology or plates with unfavorable orientation. It could be shown that fundamental toughening mechanisms are also active in additive manufactured NiAl-(Cr,Mo) composites even down to the size of nano-structured plates.

title: Niobium partitioning-mediated austenite decomposition in a Si-modified austenitic stainless steel during long-term thermal aging at 550 °C
Twin boundary modification induced by dopant segregation
Micromechanics of the sintering force in sintering by bulk diffusion
Programmable polar vortex lattices as nano-transducers for sub-terahertz coherent phonon excitation
abstract: Sub-terahertz elastic waves enable electromechanical and magnetoacoustic interactions at the nanometer spatial and picosecond temporal scales, and hold promising prospects for next-generation sensing, imaging and signal-processing techniques. However, their nanometric wavelengths impose great challenges on materials design and experimental accessibility. Here, we demonstrated that polar vortex lattices in ferroelectric thin films can act as programable transducers to generate sub-terahertz elastic waves (coherent phonons), whose frequency can be tuned by varying the film thickness. Leveraging the intrinsic nonlinearity of ferroelectrics and the multiple spatial modes of vortex lattices, higher-frequency waves are achieved via high-order harmonic generation and coherent overtones. Notably, electric-field tuning of vortex lattices enables dynamic amplitude modulation by over an order of magnitude. Moreover, the chiral vortex lattice enables frequency-selective excitation of Rayleigh and shear-horizontal waves. This behavior originates from nanoscale polarization modulations within polar vortex lattices, which induce spatially periodic stresses that are phase-matched with high-wavevector acoustic modes. Our findings shed new insights into the interplay between collective dynamics of polar topological textures and coherent phonons, opening avenues for sub-terahertz elastic-wave technologies.

title: Kinematic analysis of shear localization in lath martensite under bending based on a non-symmetric displacement gradient framework
Influence of magnetic phase transition and magnetic structure on cryogenic magnetocaloric effect in metamagnetic Ho3Si2C2 compound
Negative thermal expansion of Barium Copper Silicate
Simultaneous enhancement of coercivity and electric resistivity of Nd-Fe-B magnets by Tb2O3 stepwise reduction-grain boundary diffusion process
Strain-rate dependent screw dislocation glide mechanisms in BCC refractory metals and alloys
Local lattice distortion governs stochastic dislocation-twin boundary interactions in fcc alloys
Microbial degradation of the passive films drives corrosion of Ti-6Al-4 V by sulfate-reducing bacteria in seawater
Spatially resolved structural correlations at the nanoscale in phase-separated silicate glass revealed by electron total scattering analysis using 4D-STEM
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding structural heterogeneity in silicate glasses at the nanometer scale remains challenging because conventional diffraction techniques provide only a spatially averaged structural response and cannot resolve the atomic structure of individual amorphous domains. Here, spatially resolved electron total scattering is used to investigate a phase-separated soda–lime–silicate glass by combining local Selected-Area Electron Diffraction (SAED) and four-dimensional Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (4D-STEM). Electron diffraction data were processed using the ePDFMapping software package to obtain electron pair distribution functions (ePDFs). Local SAED measurements reveal two distinct phase-specific structural signatures corresponding to silica-rich droplets and the surrounding modifier-rich matrix. While both phases exhibit similar tetrahedral short-range order, they differ systematically in their medium-range organization, the most prominent feature being a shift of the First Sharp Diffraction Peak (FSDP). Spatially resolved 4D-STEM reproduces this structural contrast and directly maps its spatial distribution across individual amorphous domains at the nanometer scale through Pearson-correlation analysis of both reciprocal-space S ( Q ) and real-space G ( r ) , together with peak position and integrated-area analyses. The close agreement with SAED demonstrates that 4D-STEM provides sufficient sensitivity to resolve these phase-dependent structural signatures while enabling their spatial localization. Conventional bulk X-ray total scattering contains the structural contributions of both amorphous phases only as an averaged response, whereas spatially resolved electron total scattering separates and maps these contributions directly. These results establish spatially resolved electron total scattering as a powerful approach for probing nanoscale variations in medium-range order in heterogeneous glasses and other amorphous materials.

title: Dislocation locking versus distributed amorphization: Crystallographic dichotomy of fracture in GaSb
Tuning grain-boundary cohesion and chemical ordering via trace boron in BCC Ti-Al-Nb alloy
Grain boundary migration across compositional complexity: A molecular dynamics study from binary alloys to high-entropy alloys
abstract: Grain boundary (GB) migration critically influences the mechanical response of structural metals, making a mechanistic understanding of this process indispensable. GB migration in binary alloys has been extensively examined within the framework of the Cahn--L\"{u}cke--St\"{u}we (CLS) theory. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), composed of more than four principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions, have recently attracted considerable attention as next-generation structural materials because of their excellent mechanical performance, including superior high-temperature strength compared with pure metals and conventional binary alloys. However, the multicomponent nature of HEAs raises questions about the applicability of the CLS theory, and the mechanisms underlying their exceptional mechanical properties remain incompletely understood. To achieve a unified understanding of GB migration across compositional complexity from binary alloys to HEAs, we employed a combined approach integrating the CLS framework with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of GB migration. The MD simulations demonstrate that, similar to binary alloy models, GB migration resistance in the HEA model increases due to solute drag arising from dynamic elemental segregation to the moving boundary. Applying the CLS theory with a modified solute-diffusion profile to the binary alloy model leads to quantitative agreement between the simulated and predicted migration resistance. In contrast, the migration resistance in the HEA model cannot be quantitatively explained by the modified CLS theory alone, indicating the involvement of additional mechanisms. We propose that local compositional heterogeneity near the GB, which arises naturally from the compositional complexity of multicomponent alloys, constitutes an additional and distinct source of GB migration resistance unique to HEAs.

title: Insights into hydrogen-induced vacancy stability and creep in chemically complex alloys
abstract: Hydrogen (H) content modifies the creep response of Fe-based alloys by altering thermodynamics of point-defects; here we identify the electronic-structure mechanism underlying this effect. Using spin-polarized first-principles calculations combined with a cluster dynamics formulation, we establish a general framework linking H-assisted vacancy stabilization to diffusion-mediated creep in BCC Fe, FCC Fe, and chemically complex FCC Fe-Cr-Ni alloys. H-vacancy binding analysis shows that H-stabilized vacancies form at low hydrogen content in BCC Fe but require much higher chemical potentials in FCC Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloys due to broader d-bands, electronic screening, and chemical disorder. Consequently, plastic deformation mediated by diffusive processes is expected to be far more strongly impacted in BCC Fe than in FCC alloys. These electronic-controlled trends determine steady-state vacancy populations and provide a symmetry-resolved microscopic basis for H-assisted creep in ferritic and austenitic steels.

title: Editorial Board
Metalloid silicon alloying enables ultrastrong and ductile single-phase high-entropy alloys
Effect of stacking complexity on deformation and fracture of hexagonal SiC polytypes: An atomistic investigation
abstract: Stacking-sequence variations in polytypic silicon carbide (SiC) provide a unique platform to isolate the influence of long-range structural order on mechanical behavior while preserving identical local tetrahedral Si–C bonding. However, the mechanistic role of stacking sequence in governing shear instability, strain localization, and fracture in hexagonal SiC remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the tensile deformation behavior along the 〈 1120 〉 direction of 2H, 4H, and 6H SiC using molecular dynamics simulations with a machine-learning interatomic potential (UF3). All polytypes show nearly identical elastic responses up to 6% strain. However, significant differences emerge near failure. To understand these differences, we examine the evolution of shear localization using von Mises strain and non-affine squared displacement. Deformation in all polytypes is governed by shear, while the degree of localization varies significantly. Shear localization severity follows the order 4 H > 6 H > 2 H . This trend mirrors the corresponding increase in Shannon entropy–based local stacking complexity, suggesting that higher local stacking heterogeneity promotes stronger strain localization in hexagonal SiC. In contrast, peak tensile stress follows the order 6 H > 4 H > 2 H and correlates with unstable stacking fault energy and theoretical shear strength obtained from generalized stacking fault energy calculations. These results demonstrate that global hexagonality governs intrinsic shear resistance and attainable peak stress, whereas local stacking complexity controls strain localization and fracture morphology.

title: Synergistic effects of soft-hard spots in Ni-Co-P nanoglass boost superior electrocatalytic activity
Hydrogen sorption-induced tuning of magnetocaloric properties of heavy rare-earth-based Laves-phase DyCo2 for hydrogen liquefaction
abstract: Materials with magnetic phase transitions in the cryogenic temperature range are the key for efficient magnetocaloric hydrogen liquefaction. The Laves-phase DyCo 2 exhibits a significant magnetocaloric effect, but its Curie temperature ( T C ) is above the temperature window needed to magnetically liquefy hydrogen. Here the change of its T C upon hydrogen absorption was investigated. Complete hydrogenation modified T C from 139 K to 24 K, leading to 3.4 hydrogen atoms per unit cell of the crystal. Partial hydrogenation leads to two distinct T C ’s, corresponding to the parent and hydrogenated phase. Light microscopy revealed a maze-like pattern on the micron scale for the DyCo 2 phase, which is not found for the materials saturated in hydrogen, and a core–shell-like microstructure was observed in the partially hydrogenated samples, where the pattern of DyCo 2 phase is only seen on the core. The Hydrogen-sorption reactions yield a massive crystal volume increase of 21%. After thermal dehydrogenation T C was recovered, however stacking faults and chemical heterogeneities were detected by high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy, which reduced magnetocaloric performance of the dehydrogenated compound. The isothermal entropy change reached up to 21 J kg -1 K -1 in the pristine DyCo 2 when 14 T magnetic field was applied at 139 K, while the fully hydrogenated compound reached 15 J kg -1 K -1 at 24 K. Our work demonstrates the usefulness of reversible hydrogen sorption to tune the magnetocaloric properties of heavy rare-earth-based Laves-phases towards hydrogen liquefaction transition temperature range.

title: Achieving wide axial zero thermal expansion and enhanced toughness by microstructure orientation engineering
Fracture induced by a martensitic grain boundary complexion transition
Volume, grain- and interphase-boundary diffusion of Ag in eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 compositionally complex alloy
abstract: Solute diffusion of Ag in a two-phase multi-principal element eutectic AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy is measured in an extended temperature interval using the radiotracer technique. Both volume and short-circuit diffusion rates of Ag are determined. Complementary ToF-SIMS and high-resolution STEM experiments with natural Ag are used to distinguish the diffusion paths in the eutectic microstructure, especially to quantify the relative contributions of interphase and grain boundaries. Furthermore, Ag diffusion is measured in single-phase FCC and B2-ordered alloys with compositions mimicking those in the eutectic material. The results are analyzed accounting for the chemical complexity of the contributing phases and discussed with respect to the ”sluggish” diffusion concept proposed originally for high entropy alloys.

title: Solid-state grain-boundary defect-phase formation in the Fe–Zn system
abstract: Liquid metal embrittlement (LME) of next generation galvanized steels has recently been shown to involve intermetallic phase formation at preferably high-angle grain-boundaries (HAGB) prior to microcracking. These GB phases emerge already at temperatures much below the melting point of Zn and point towards the importance of solid-state GB mechanisms. To better isolate such early GB phase formation, we pursue here in-situ heating inside a transmission electron microscope on a HAGB of a Fe-Zn solid solution model system. Clear Zn segregation in the HAGB is seen, followed by the formation of an L1 0 FeZn GB phase. Being not part of the equilibrium phase diagram, this phase is considered as a defect phase. Complementing density functional theory calculations demonstrate how the unexpected phase can be energetically favored inside a GB. In concert with bulk synchrotron diffraction data, we propose that this defect phase is an intermediate state towards the higher Zn-containing Fe 3 Zn 10 phase that otherwise is dominating revealed GB intermetallics during the early stages of LME in galvanized steels.

title: A framework for structure–energy mapping of compact nanovoid–solute complexes: Tungsten alloys as model systems
Gradient amorphous interphases toughen ultrastrong nanolayered metals by regulating dislocation storage and mobility
Fault architecture-controlled γ↔ε transformation and reversion under strain-controlled fatigue in a metastable high-entropy alloy
Enhanced cryogenic strength–ductility synergy via Mn-tuned ε-martensite topology control in Ni–Co–Cr–Mo multi-principal element alloys
Cr substitution in NASICON cathodes unlocks V4+/V5+ redox and intermediate-phase evolution for high-energy and stable sodium storage
Formation mechanisms of meso-scale element segregation in multi-material metal additive manufacturing
Grain boundary-stress fundamental zones: A systematic exploration of orientation-dependent material response
abstract: The description of the symmetries inherent to grain boundaries has made it possible to probe the vast orientation space linked to these interfaces. However, under any given stress state, exploring the space of distinct configurations (with a total of 8 degrees of freedom) remains impractical. Taking advantage of the grain boundary and stress tensor symmetries, the current work shows that for every bicrystal there exists a fundamental zone that uniquely captures all possible stress orientations. These regions are systematically derived for axisymmetric and triaxial stresses in S2 and SO(3) spaces, respectively. Computational tools for cubic materials with Oh point group symmetry are also provided to facilitate the adoption of grain boundary-stress fundamental zones. Among other advantages, this approach provides a significant reduction in the size of the orientation domain, enhanced visualization of orientation-dependent material performance, and statistical analyses of mechanical response via weighted distributions over the entire configuration space. Together with an elastic bicrystal stress incompatibility model, a series of case studies reveals insights into the role of elastic anisotropy on damage distribution, invalidates prior assumptions related to the origins of slip localization near Σ3 coherent twin boundaries, and showcases a new way to optimize the orientation of textured materials with respect to a remote stress. All of this represents an important step towards the systematic identification and exploration of critical grain boundary configurations for arbitrary materials and stress states.

title: Atomic-flux tunable exchange-spring magnetism in SmFe12/Fe nanocomposites
A dual-precipitation strategy for tailoring the strengths of ferrite and martensite in dual-phase steels
abstract: Conventional strengthening strategies for ferrite–martensite dual-phase (DP) steels generally focus on strengthening individual constituent phases, often increasing the strength mismatch between ferrite and martensite and thereby limiting mechanical performance. Here, we propose a dual-precipitation strategy that enables simultaneous precipitation strengthening of both ferrite and martensite through controlled phase transformation followed by tempering. This approach introduces two distinct precipitate populations: interphase precipitates in ferrite and tempering-induced precipitates in martensite. Precipitation behaviour in Ti microalloyed steels, with and without Mo addition, was systematically investigated across varying ferrite–martensite fractions using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), small-angle neutron scattering (SANS), and atom probe tomography (APT). Increasing ferrite fraction progressively reduces precipitation sensitivity during tempering, producing coarser precipitates with lower number density. Mo addition primarily promotes early-stage precipitate nucleation rather than substantially enhancing coarsening resistance, resulting in higher precipitate densities and enhanced strengthening. Precipitate chemistry exhibits pronounced size dependence, with smaller precipitates being increasingly metal-rich, while Mo promotes carbon vacancy incorporation within B1-type precipitates. Strengthening estimation indicates that even ultrafine precipitates strengthen the material predominantly through the Orowan bypassing mechanism. These findings demonstrate that dual-precipitation strategy provides a new microstructural design strategy for tailoring phase-specific strengthening and strength mismatch, offering opportunities to optimise the balance between strength and formability in advanced DP steels.

title: Contribution of chemically disordered second phases and coherent interfaces to the biased defect flow at the early stage of irradiation in steels
Predicting glass-forming ability in binary alloys by machine learning
Microbiologically influenced corrosion of metallic materials: Microstructure, coupled degradation mechanisms, and protection
Nano-scale Portevin – Le Chatelier effect in Al-Mg alloys
abstract: Serrated deformation behavior in Al-Mg alloys, commonly associated with the Portevin-Le Châtelier (PLC) effect at macroscopic scales, originates from dynamic strain aging (DSA) at microscopic scales. However, the underlying nanoscale mechanisms bridging this gap between macroscopic and microscopic scales remain unclear. In this study, indentation experiments combined with transmission electron microscopy were employed to directly correlate deformation behavior with solute-dislocation interactions in Al-Mg alloys. Low-angle tilt grain boundaries (LAtGBs) were formed beneath indent edges, where the tensile strain fields around edge-dislocations were decorated with Mg. Screw dislocation networks were confirmed between leading and trailing LAtGBs, and the misorientation of LAtGBs evolved through the incorporation of these screw dislocations. The present results demonstrate that serrated deformation in Al-Mg alloys arises from the intermittent migration of LAtGBs coupled with collective dislocation transport by screw dislocation networks, providing a nanoscale mechanism linking solute-dislocation interactions to macroscopic plastic instability.

title: Dislocation-mediated continuous precipitation in Mo-bearing martensitic steel: from solute co-segregation and coherent precursors to α-M2C carbides
abstract: The precipitation of M 2 C in Mo-bearing martensitic steels during tempering has often been described as a classical M 3 C → M 2 C transformation, despite the crystallographic and compositional incompatibilities this path entails with respect to the martensitic matrix. Here, by combining high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), three-dimensional atom probe tomography (3D-APT), and first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we reveal a dislocation-mediated sequence during tempering at 700°C: solute co-segregation at screw dislocations, formation of Mo-rich coherent precursors, development of a 5R intermediate phase with AABBB/ABCAB stacking, and formation of orthorhombic α-M 2 C. DFT explains that C segregates first to screw dislocation cores and subsequently attracts Mo via strong C–Mo chemical binding (∼0.6 eV), leading to cooperative C-assisted Mo segregation. The resulting coherent precursors (∼40 at.% Mo) provide a BCC-derived framework for stacking reconstruction: continued C insertion drives local planes toward close-packed geometry, enabling nucleation of a local BBB close-packed embryo at the coherent precursor/matrix interface and growth into an AABBB 5R structure; further C enrichment promotes basal partial-dislocation glide, converting AABBB to a faulted ABCAB variant. As the composition approaches (Mo+Cr):C ≈ 2:1, the modulation and fault arrays are eliminated, producing a relatively defect-free metal sublattice with ABAB-stacked α-M 2 C. A first-principles relative formation-energy map shows that the 5R occupies a metastable energy basin between the coherent precursor and α-M 2 C, supporting energetically gradual precursor-mediated route. This pathway provides an additional, crystallographically grounded alternative to the classical M 3 C → M 2 C model and offers new insights for designing nano-precipitate microstructures in advanced steels.

title: Superior cryogenic strength-ductility synergy in a crack-free additively manufactured multicomponent L12-strengthened medium-entropy alloy
abstract: Developing advanced ultrastrong-yet-ductile structural alloys at both room and cryogenic temperatures is a long-standing challenge in the materials community. In this study, we present an integrated strategy combining compositional design with additive manufacturing (AM) to fabricate a medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a high L1 2 vol fraction (∼44.2%) via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The newly designed alloy exhibits excellent printability with a high relative density of 99.97%. Thermodynamic and thermal-fluid simulations reveal that the extremely high cooling rate (∼7 × 10 6 K/s), steep temperature gradient (∼7 × 10 7 K/m), and narrow solidification range (248 K). It promotes a single-phase face-centered-cubic (FCC) solidification path while reducing cracking susceptibility. Upon the post-heat treatment, coherent L1 2 nanoparticles are controllably introduced, producing a distinctive dual-phase microstructure. The heat-treated MEA (HT-MEA) exhibits exceptional tensile properties with a yield strength (σ y ) of 1240 MPa and an ultimate tensile strength (σ u ) of 1646 MPa, combined with a ductility of 25.0% at room temperature. More prominently, the σ y and σ u further increase to 1413 MPa and 2011 MPa at 77 K accompanied by the uniform elongation of 27.3%. Detailed microstructural examinations indicate that the temperature-dependent mechanical responses originate from the sequential activations of various deformation substructures. These findings demonstrate a new alloy design paradigm that realizes both superior mechanical properties and excellent AM printability, which could effectively empower the development of advanced structural materials operable under extreme service conditions.

title: M-site 3d-orbital hybridization in Cr2AlB2 for synergistically enhanced microwave absorption and oxidation resistance
Resolving the multifaceted diffusion mechanisms in Nd-Fe-B magnets via in-situ heating TEM
Thermodynamics and dynamics of non-compact prismatic dislocation loops simulated using a machine-learning model
abstract: We explore how the thermodynamic properties and dynamics of a self-interstitial prismatic dislocation loop are affected by microscopic-scale variations in its geometric configuration, an aspect that rarely received attention in literature. We develop a machine-learning (ML) model to predict the formation energy of an arbitrary geometrically complex configuration of a self-interstitial atom dislocation loop. Trained on atomistic simulation data, the ML model achieves high predictive accuracy across a broad range of configurations, with a typical error in the 1% range. From the ML model, we evaluate the density of configurational microstates as a function of loop's formation energy and derive analytical expressions valid in tractable limiting cases. Using statistical mechanics, we derive the configurational free energy, the average energy, and the thermodynamic entropy of a dislocation loop as a function of temperature. We also simulate the dynamics of self-climb of dislocation loops with various geometries and evaluate their diffusion coefficients and effective activation energy for diffusion. Analysis shows that there is a single universal parameter describing the morphological irregularity of the loop configuration in its ground state. This parameter determines the thermodynamic properties of a loop as well as its dynamics, and simulations illustrate how the properties and mobility of a configurationally complex loop vary as functions of the irregularity parameter.

title: Phase stability and synthesis of Na4Ti5O12 in the Na2O-TiO2 system: CALPHAD modeling and experiment
Autonomous mechanism discovery in tough alloy design via causal reinforcement learning on knowledge graphs
abstract: The design of tough alloys as maraging steels was mainly explored by integrated computational materials engineering and domain-knowledge guided artificial intelligence (AI), relying critically on the introduction of accurate physical mechanisms. However, the discovery and quantification of mechanisms remain dependent on time-consuming experimental characterization and expert interpretation, which are prone to subjective bias. These challenges are limiting the accuracy and efficiency of the design of alloys with satisfactory toughness. Here, we propose a causal reinforcement learning framework based on dynamic knowledge graphs for the autonomous discovery of mechanisms directly from reported literature data. In this framework, a reinforcement learning agent iteratively prunes the graph, guided by causal principles to identify influential relationships, while predictive improvement is used as the reward. Applied to ultrahigh-strength maraging steels, the framework learned from high-quality literature data and autonomously uncovered the mechanistic chain “Mo content → interfacial energy → toughness”, which is easily overlooked in conventional approached. Guided by this mechanism, the AI framework identified multiple alloy candidates with excellent strength–toughness synergy. Moreover, the model showed strong generalization ability, maintaining high predictive accuracy in both out-of-domain and data-scarce regimes where conventional models suffered severe performance degradation. By this knowledge-led AI strategy, the toughness-controlling mechanisms can be automatically summarized from literature data, which can greatly reduce the complexity of revealing mechanisms through experimental methods and accelerate the development efficiency of tough alloys. This method can be extended to other performance designs involving controversial mechanisms.

title: From loop emission to dislocation jamming: Contrasting nanoindentation-induced plasticity in wurtzite ZnO and GaN
abstract: Dislocations govern plastic deformation in crystalline solids and also strongly influence the functional performance of semiconductor crystals. Nanoindentation provides a localized and controllable route for introducing dislocations, even in materials that are brittle at the bulk scale, and can generate nontrivial dislocation configurations under appropriate conditions. Here, we examine the dislocation structures generated by nanoindentation in two wurtzite semiconductors, GaN and ZnO, indented on the (0001) 45° off plane. In GaN, dislocations exhibit strong mutual interactions and jamming, leading to an entangled three-dimensional tube-like morphology. In contrast, ZnO predominantly develops a one-dimensional array of dislocation loops. The emission of multiple discrete dislocation loops produces multiple pop-ins in the load-depth curve of ZnO, whereas only a single pop-in occurs in GaN. Dislocations in ZnO extend much deeper into the crystal than those in GaN, indicating less effective local strain accommodation than in GaN, where dislocation entanglement and jamming enhance the back stress. In addition, 1 / 3 < 11 2 ¯ 3 > pyramidal dislocations are activated at relatively small normalized indentation depths in GaN, whereas in ZnO they appear only at larger normalized depths in the simulations and are not retained in post-mortem experimental observations. These results demonstrate that the shared wurtzite structure alone does not determine the indentation-induced dislocation architecture; rather, material-specific lattice resistance, dislocation interactions, and back-stress evolution control the plastic response and the resulting opportunities for dislocation engineering.

title: Dynamic deprotonation drives interfacial pH self-buffering enables ultrastable oxygen evolution in pentlandite

Kinetics of low temperature dislocation plasticity in a refractory multi-principal element alloy
abstract: A rigorous identification of the temperature-dependent, rate-controlling dislocation mechanisms and their associated kinetics in refractory multi-principal element alloys (RMPEAs) is fundamental to the development of predictive strengthening frameworks. In this work, we isolate single-slip { 110 } 〈 111 〉 plasticity in the BCC RMPEA Hf 10 Mo 10 Nb 35 Ta 20 Ti 25 (at.%) using orientation-controlled micropillar compression between 200–300 K and strain rates from 1 0 − 3 to 1 0 2 s − 1 . The adherence to a single-slip condition enables direct determination of the temperature and strain-rate dependence of the critical resolved shear stress and the associated activation parameters. By combining transmission electron microscopy, phase-field dislocation dynamics (PFDD) simulations, and analytical strengthening models, the governing dislocation-mediated plasticity mechanism and its temperature evolution are identified. The results establish the rate-limiting role of screw dislocations, quantify the relative mobility of edge and screw segments, and assess the predictive capability of existing analytical models. The convergence between experiments, theoretical models and PFDD simulations provides a mechanistically consistent framework for understanding temperature-dependent plasticity in chemically complex BCC alloys and advances the development of physics-based strengthening descriptions for RMPEAs.

title: Suppression of skin-effect-enhanced magnetic viscosity for ultralow-loss MHz soft magnetic composites
The interfacial deformation pathways governed by characteristic CeAlSi phases regulate the hot workability of Al-Mg-Si alloys
Rare-earth-free Fe2P-based compounds: Tuning and modeling of hard magnetic properties
abstract: Fe 2 − x Co x P 1 − y Si y has attracted significant attention for permanent magnet applications due to its promising intrinsic magnetic properties and the absence of strategic elements such as rare earths. To date, most samples reported in the literature are polycrystalline and obtained via mechanical alloying, which makes direct measurement of magnetocrystalline anisotropy particularly challenging. In contrast, only a limited number of single-crystal compositions have been investigated. In this work, Fe 2 − x Co x P 1 − y Si y polycrystalline samples were synthesized by combined induction and arc melting techniques. Compared with mechanically alloyed materials reported in the literature, the resulting samples exhibit a higher degree of phase purity, with secondary phases appearing only in specimens with high Si content. The composition dependence of the intrinsic magnetic properties, namely Curie temperature, saturation magnetization, and magnetocrystalline anisotropy, was systematically investigated over the compositional range 0.1 ≤ x ≤ 0.3 and 0.1 ≤ y ≤ 0.4 , extending beyond the range previously explored in single crystals. The anisotropy field was directly measured on polycrystalline samples by means of the Singular Point Detection technique in pulsed magnetic fields. The maximum anisotropy field μ 0 H A = 2.84 T was found for Fe 1.90 Co 0.10 P 0.80 Si 0.20 , which also exhibits a saturation magnetization M S = 111 A m 2 /kg and a Curie temperature T C = 495 K. All investigated compounds display a magnetic hardness parameter κ > 1 and tunable intrinsic magnetic properties. The theoretical maximum energy product approaches 200 kJ/m comparable to values obtained for single crystals. These characteristics, together with the possibility of obtaining nearly single-phase materials through scalable melting routes, make this compound family one of the most promising candidates for rare-earth-free permanent magnets with performance intermediate between ferrites and rare-earth magnets. Experimental results were complemented by density functional theory calculations, which were used to map the magnetic moment and magnetocrystalline anisotropy energy over a broader compositional space. The calculations reveal that band filling plays a crucial role in optimizing the anisotropy and overall magnetic performance of the Fe 2 − x Co x P 1 − y Si y system.

title: Effect of silicon substrate orientations and deposition conditions on the nucleation and morphological evolution of diamond crystals
The calculation of kinetic interface contact condition phase diagram during the melting of multi-component alloys
abstract: Despite the differences between solid and liquid phase in both structural and diffusional kinetic aspects, the kinetic processes at a migrating solid-liquid interface are common for solidification and melting. It is demonstrated in this contribution that the three-kinetic-process solute drag and trapping model, proposed by the author recently for rapid solidification, is applicable to calculating the interface contact conditions during melting. The model implementation is shared via a copy-left license. The model is employed to calculate the kinetic melting phase diagrams of a binary ideal A-B solid solution system, a Succinonitrile(SCN)-Water system, a binary Al-Mg alloy, and a multi-component Alnico alloy. To compare with the reported experimental melting rate results in the literature and verify the calculated kinetic phase diagram, the kinetic phase diagram is used together with the analytical solution of the diffusion equation within the bulk phases to calculate melting rate. The calculated results are compared and interpreted with the experimental results. For a given melting temperature, with the increase of the interface velocity, the proposed model predicts the kinetic solidus and liquidus moves towards each other. Meanwhile, they will be shifted upwards. When the interface velocity is low, local equilibrium is a good assumption. The proposed model also gives a detailed description of the interfacial solutal melting process. The kinetic phase diagram could be used further as the boundary conditions for numerical melting rate calculation models. For the future work, the calculation of interfacial diffusive speed parameters for multi-component aluminum alloys with MD simulation will be pursued.

title: Why high entropy alloys may decompose slower: Misalignment of early-pathways and equilibrium stages
abstract: The notion of slow decomposition in high entropy alloys (HEAs, also known as multi-principal element alloys, or more broadly as chemically complex materials) has been extensively discussed in relation to higher configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion, as possible origins of stability. However, both assumptions have been critically reassessed in recent years. Here, we reveal a hidden kinetic barrier that arises during multi-component decomposition when thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic transport pathways are misaligned in the composition space. We develop a CALPHAD-integrated, multi-component Cahn–Hilliard framework and software to determine the characteristic time of linear decomposition (CTLD) from the fastest-growing coupled eigenmode, and compare it with an effective estimate obtained by projecting kinetics onto the thermodynamic instability. Studying the Fe–Mn–Ni–Co–Cu alloy system, we show that the eigenproblem systematically yields a longer CTLD than the effective projection, demonstrating that thermo-kinetic mode rotation delays early-stage amplification even without invoking intrinsically reduced atomic mobilities. We further quantify the degree of misalignment between growth modes and equilibrium tie-lines, revealing a potential of kinetic frustration that prolongs the time to reach equilibrium compositions beyond the linear regime. We discuss our results in comparison with experimental measurements and consistently predict early-stage length and time scales for the formation of Cu clusters during rapid quenching. The present theoretical framework enables fast, high-throughput evaluation of phase stability in HEAs and other multi-component alloys.

title: The entropy of “High-entropy” alloys of transition metals with aluminum
Enhancement of damping constant in Nd-doped L10-FePt at elevated temperatures for HAMR
abstract: Hard disk drives (HDDs) are main storage devices in data centers handling petabyte-scale AI data, and achieving higher recording density with heat-assisted magnetic recording (HAMR) requires media material design that ensures a sufficiently large damping constant ( α ) at elevated temperatures to enable reliable magnetization reversal. We investigated Nd-doped L1 0 -FePt continuous films to clarify the effect of rare-earth element doping on α at elevated temperatures where recording occurs. (FePt) 100-x (Nd) x thin films with Nd content ranging from 0.0 to 4.1 at.% were prepared by sputtering and characterized for microstructure and magnetic properties. Nd was completely rejected from FePt, and Nd and Pt segregated into Fe-deficient void regions in the FePt layer. Nevertheless, enhanced spin-orbit coupling (SOC) locally at the FePt/Nd interface increased magnetic anisotropy with a small amount of Nd doping. The magnetization dynamics were measured by time-resolved magneto-optical Kerr effect (TRMOKE) from room temperature to near T C . Effective α near T C increased from 0.048 (undoped) to 0.066 (Nd 4.1 at.%). These findings demonstrate that rare-earth element doping can modulate α even in FePt, which already exhibits strong SOC, and highlight a media design strategy to optimize α for HAMR performance.

title: Identification of active site with activity-stability trade-off in Fe-incorporated NiOOH for oxygen evolution
Influence of strength contrast between austenite and martensite on the yield point elongation phenomenon in a metastable austenitic stainless steel

Long-term relaxation and nucleation in a far-from-equilibrium glass
abstract: Previous studies have indicated that the kinetics of crystal nucleation below the glass transition region are strongly affected by the relaxation of the glass structure during aging, making the nucleation rate a highly sensitive probe for monitoring this process. In this study, we confirmed this result by supplementing nucleation kinetics measurements in lithium disilicate glass aged at 663 K (64 K below the standard glass transition temperature, T g ) for up to 454 days with measurements of several properties for the first time. We detected subtle systematic increases in the first-heating T g onset and enthalpy recovery at advanced relaxation stages, whereas the ionic conductivity continued to decrease for at least four months of aging. Density measurements, however, were unable to resolve the subtle changes occurring at advanced relaxation stages due to experimental uncertainty. Structural relaxation was confirmed by Raman spectroscopy, which indicated a redistribution of Q -species over time. The most relevant result is that the increase in the Q 3 species content correlates with the decrease in the structural order parameter ζ , which is introduced into the classical nucleation theory equations to quantitatively describe the nucleation kinetics during relaxation. Since the Q 3 species are the characteristic silicate units of the ideal lithium disilicate crystal structure, we hypothesize that their increase during relaxation likely contributes to the decrease in the interfacial surface energy, leading to the observed increase in the nucleation rate.

title: Thermodynamic stability of Al/MgZn2 interfaces including vibrational entropy and thermal expansion contributions
abstract: The surface energies of Al(111) and MgZn 2 (0001) slabs, as well as the interface energies of the Al(111)||MgZn 2 (0001) interfaces with different terminations and stacking orders were calculated using a combination of first-principles and phonon calculations under the assumptions of the harmonic and quasi-harmonic approximations. The thermodynamic stabilities of slabs and interfaces at 0 K and finite temperatures were analyzed by considering the effects of vibrational entropy and volume. It is found that the surface energies decreased with temperature as a result of vibrational entropy and thermal expansion, which led to an additional -but limited- reduction on the free energy that did not change the thermodynamic stability of the surface slabs. The interface energy of the interfaces also decreased with temperature due to the vibrational entropy, while thermal expansion provided an additional positive or negative contribution to the interface energy. As a result, the thermodynamic stability of the interfaces changed depending on whether thermal expansion was considered. The effect of bond stiffness and thermal expansion on the surface and interface energies was discussed. This investigation provides a clear strategy to assess the effect of temperature and volumetric changes on the thermodynamic properties of surfaces and interfaces.

title: Cluster expansion modeling of phase stability in CrTaVW high entropy alloys with small Hf additions to guide experimental design
abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys are promising candidates for radiation-tolerant materials, with certain refractory compositions showing suppressed defect-cluster formation under irradiation. Although CrTaVW has exhibited favorable irradiation resistance, its manufacturing remains a major challenge. In this work, we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations with the cluster expansion (CE) method to develop a predictive thermodynamic model for CrTaVW-based refractory HEAs, using small Hf additions as a compositional tuning strategy. Using this model, we investigate the equilibrium phase behavior of different subsystems containing 1–5 at.% Hf and determine the order–disorder transition temperature (ODTT) for each composition. The results show that the effect of Hf addition on the ODTT is composition dependent. In some subsystems, the ODTT remains nearly unchanged with Hf addition, whereas in others, even low Hf concentrations increase the ODTT. These results provide guidance for future experimental studies on the thermodynamic stability and thermomechanical properties of irradiation-resistant refractory alloys.

title: MagnoCluster: A physics-informed unsupervised learning framework for interpretable classification of magnetocaloric materials

Tellurium trioxide as an n-type wide-gap semiconductor with ultrahigh work functions from first principles
abstract: ABSTRACT The exploration of next-generation wide-gap semiconductors with extreme work functions is highly desirable for the continued advancement of electronic and optoelectronic devices. By using first principles calculations, we show that β- TeO 3 , with a wide band gap exceeding 3 eV, emerges as a promising n-type semiconductor exhibiting ultrahigh work functions of up to ∼8 eV. Intentionally or unintentionally incorporated interstitial H, Li, Na, Cu, Mg, and Zn impurities and substitutional F impurities are identified as shallow donors, whereas O vacancies act as minor carrier-compensating defects that locally trap electrons at neighbouring Te sites. The work function is evaluated across a series of low-index nonpolar surfaces. The presence of ordered O vacancies is energetically favoured on these surfaces and tends to reduce the corresponding work functions. These findings underscore the significance of precise control over the O chemical potential to suppress surface O-vacancy formation, thereby preserving the exceptional electronic performance of β- TeO 3 associated with ultrahigh work functions. Collectively, the results highlight the potential of β- TeO 3 for hole injection/extraction/transport layers as well as transparent electrodes for applications such as light-emitting devices and photovoltaic cells, while providing useful guidance on carrier doping and surface tuning for these practical applications through elucidating the effects of the point-defect and surface configurations on the electronic properties.

title: Hydrogen trapping at γ′ and γ″ precipitates in nickel and its alloys
Microstructure evolution during rapid solidification of hypoeutectic Al-Ag alloys near absolute stability
Beyond Vegard’s Law: Short-Range Structural Heterogeneity in Gd₂O₃–UO₂ Fuel and Its Impact on Thermophysical Properties
abstract: Gadolinium oxide (Gd₂O₃) is widely used as a burnable neutron absorber in uranium dioxide (UO2) fuel, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing its impact on thermophysical performance remains elusive. Here, we establish a direct structure-property relationship in Gd-doped UO₂ (mass fractions of 6 % – 15 % Gd), by integrating X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM/EDS), synchrotron-based Extended X-ray Absorption Fine Structure (EXAFS), resonant ultrasound spectroscopy (RUS), and thermophysical property measurements. XRD results confirm the formation of a single-phase fluorite solid solution with a linear lattice contraction following Vegard’s law, while EXAFS reveals local distortions, oxygen vacancies, and nanoscale bixbyite Gd₂O₃-like environments undetectable by bulk methods. Microstructural analysis shows homogeneous Gd distribution without secondary phases or microcracking with higher dopant levels reducing grain size and increasing porosity. Thermophysical measurements demonstrate that Gd incorporation significantly decreases thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity, particularly at lower temperatures, due to enhanced phonon–defect scattering. Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy further reveals a progressive reduction in elastic stiffness with increasing Gd content, consistent with defect-induced lattice softening. Thermal resistivity analysis indicates that impurity scattering dominates in Gd-doped UO₂, while phonon–phonon Umklapp contributions are suppressed with increasing dopant concentration. These results demonstrate the Gd-doped UO2 is globally single-phase yet locally heterogeneous, and that this short-range structural complexity governs thermal conductivity behavior. The results provide critical experimental insight for atomistically informed fuel performance models and underscore the importance of resolving local atomic environments in the evaluation of doped nuclear fuels.
