Regular meets random: A smooth connection between TPMS and Voronoi lattice in 3D printed bioceramic scaffolds
abstract: Micro-architected materials are nowadays ubiquitous in many engineering applications, where high performance and simultaneous optimization of multiple functional properties are required. In the field of bone tissue engineering, scaffolds are used to restore bone continuity within defect sites. These defects often span regions with different characteristics, ranging from cortical to trabecular bone. Consequently, an effective scaffold must incorporate spatially distinct architectural regions to mimic the heterogeneous environment of the host tissue. Combining Voronoi-based and TPMS-based architectures offers a promising strategy to recreate two fundamentally different micro-architected environments. However, a smooth and continuous transition between a regular periodic structure (TPMS) and a stochastic structure (Voronoi) has not been reported in the literature yet. In this study, a topology optimization algorithm has been employed to generate a smooth connection between the two architectures within a design composed of two concentric cylindrical regions. Finite element models were developed to identify potential stress concentrations within the hybrid scaffold: three loading conditions (i.e., uniaxial compression, radial compression, and torsion) showed that the transitional region does not exhibit high stress concentrations, confirming its structural soundness. Finally, to demonstrate the manufacturability of the proposed architecture, the scaffolds were fabricated using vat photopolymerization with hydroxyapatite and a hydroxyapatite/calcium phosphate blend. While not intended for a specific anatomical site, this design serves as a challenging test case to evaluate the printing fidelity of architectures characterized by substantially different geometrical features. In both cases, excellent printing fidelity was achieved by a proper printing parameter tuning process, as confirmed through computed micro-tomography analyses.

Critical roles of sublattice chemistry in governing mechanical behavior and deformation mechanism of L12-type chemically complex intermetallic alloys
abstract: L1 2 -type chemically complex intermetallic alloys (CCIMAs) with the ordered A 3 B structure have emerged as novel high-temperature materials due to their exceptional strength-ductility synergy and thermal stability. However, quantitative insight into the effects of sublattice chemistry on deformation and fracture mechanisms remains elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate the critical roles of the Co/Ni ratio in the A-site sublattice on the microstructure and mechanical behavior of a model Co 76.5-x Ni x Al 13.5 Ti 3 Ta 3 Nb 3.5 B 0.5 (at. %) CCIMA. All alloys exhibit fully recrystallized L1 2 -dominated grains with a small fraction of borides, indicating that their phase constitution is insensitive to the A-site chemistry. However, the Co/Ni ratio significantly influences the elemental segregation behavior at grain boundaries (GBs) and associated dislocation activities, giving rise to markedly distinct mechanical properties and fracture morphologies. An increased Co/Ni ratio reduces the anti-phase boundary (APB) energy, leading to a reduction in yield strength from ∼839 MPa (26Co-50.5Ni alloy) to ∼680 MPa (46.5Co-30Ni alloy). Concurrently, the deformation substructure evolves from APB-coupled superdislocations to superlattice intrinsic stacking faults (SISFs) and dense SISF networks, which sustains work hardening to larger strains. Moreover, in the CCIMAs with Co/Ni ≥ 1, Co enrichment accompanied by depletion of Ni and L1 2 -forming elements at GBs is associated with the formation of disordered interfacial nanolayers (DINLs) and suppressed intergranular fracture, enabling elongations exceeding ∼35% while maintaining a tensile strength of ∼1.5–1.6 GPa. This study establishes a correlation between A-site sublattice chemistry, planar fault energetics, GB chemistry/structure, and mechanical properties, providing a new paradigm for controllably designing advanced intermetallic alloys for extreme conditions.

3D Observations of Grain Growth in Textured and Untextured Undoped Alumina
abstract: The impact of grain boundary (GB) character on grain growth is assessed by studying microstructural evolution in both textured and untextured undoped alumina. Laboratory diffraction contrast tomography (LabDCT) is used to track individual grains in both microstructures across multiple heat treatment timesteps. Using this 3D data, GB character, grain morphology, GB velocity, and GB reduced mobility are measured and compared between samples slip cast inside and outside of a strong magnetic field (9T). Samples slip cast outside of the magnetic field exhibit random orientations whereas the samples slip cast in the magnetic field exhibit both crystallographic texture and a preferred GB character with a preference for the [0001] misorientation axis and (0001) plane inclination. GBs in untextured, undoped alumina migrated at a faster rate than textured, undoped alumina despite the higher average curvature found in the textured case. Furthermore, we find that low energy GBs (e.g. basal boundaries) tend to migrate at rates exceeding those of higher energy boundaries in textured alumina. Finally, we observe that both textured and untextured alumina grains adopt a slightly elongated grain morphology. The aspect ratios of untextured (1.88) and textured (2.13) alumina are relatively similar despite the high population of high mobility GBs in textured alumina. We postulate that differences in microstructural evolution between untextured and textured alumina arise due to changes in the GB network.
